subtopic: FATAL ACCIDENTS AND INJURIES FROM HIGHWAY TRAFFIC AND LEVEL CROSSINGS

speechtext: Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 27 to amend the criminal code (motor cars).

subtopic: FATAL ACCIDENTS AND INJURIES FROM HIGHWAY TRAFFIC AND LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: FATAL ACCIDENTS AND INJURIES FROM HIGHWAY TRAFFIC AND LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
The object of the bill is to call the attention of the people of Canada to the number of fatal accidents which are occurring in increasing numbers in this country. A return to an order of the house of April 3 shows that there were 149,000 accidents, and nearly 10,000 people were killed during the period covered by the return. This rate of motor car accidents on the highways is becoming a public scandal. The sections of the bill are modern and constructive in character and I hope the Minister of Justice

Criminal Code
(Mr. St. Laurent) will consider them when he is bringing in amendments to the criminal code. I shall not read the sections, but will refer only to the marginal notes.
The first section deals with the requirement that the driver of a car shall stop after an accident. Some children were killed in the riding of the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) down near the beach by a cowardly hit-and-run driver. These hit-and-run drivers are a menace all over the country. The bill provides for imprisonment for a term not less than six months without the option of a fine.
Section 2 deals with driving while under the influence of alcohol or a narcotic. The object of this section is to add the words ''under the influence of alcohol" to the section as it now stands. The next section deals also with hit-and-run drivers and provides for an increase in the penalties now imposed.
Section 5 brings the hiGand-run driver under subsection 7, and provides that an order may be made prohibiting the convicted person from driving a motor vehicle for any period not exceeding three years. The next clause deals with the causing of a death in a culpably negligent manner. This incorporates the law now in force in New York state. The amendment penalizes the driver where death results, if the driver is breaking bylaws-against speeding for instance-and where he may be thirty per cent the cause of the accident.
The next section deals with the trial of a female person. It seems only fair that in the trial of any female person by a jury a certain proportion of the jurors should be female persons. They voted 52 per cent in the elections as against a male total vote of only 48 per cent.
The marginal note for the next section reads:
Charge of manslaughter arising out of operation of motor vehicle, criminal or culpable negligence proved.
The purpose of the amendment is to define the powers of the jury in cases of manslaughter arising out of the operation of motor vehicles.
The final section defines the powers and functions of the judge and the jury by the judge. There have been instances in which cases have been taken away from the jury. Questions of law should be matters for the judge to decide, and questions of fact should be decided by the jury. The jury should decide on the evidence whether a person is guilty or not guilty.
I hope the Minister of Justice will consider these amendments to the criminal code.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT RESPECTING LIEUTENANT FRANK B. LEE

Mr. Speaker, I shall be very glad to elaborate on the answer I gave yesterday; perhaps it was too brief. I can best do so by reading a copy of a letter which I addressed to Mr. Lee:
Ottawa, April 10, 1946.
Frank B. Lee, Esq., c/o Queen's University,
Kingston, Ontario
Dear Mr. Lee:
Your letter dated March 27, addressed to the Prime Minister, has been sent to me for reply.
The regulations concerning entry into the Royal Canadian Navy permit the entry of any British subject provided he fulfils the requirements prescribed from time to time as to age, education, physical fitness, character and technical knowledge for entry into the branch or component selected. All such applications must be made to Naval Service Headquarters at Ottawa and passed on here. In connection with the examination of applications, a selection board has been created, of which Captain J. M. Grant is the president.
I have made inquiries concerning the matters dealt with in your letter of March 27 and am informed that on that date the selection board interviewed candidates from Queen's University at H.M.C.S. Cataraqui. I understand that you had made no previous application for an interview- by the board and did not appear for such an interview until the board was preparing to leave H.M.C.S. Cataraqui to catch a Toronto train and that you then approached Captain Grant as the latter was actually leaving the establishment to enter a motor car and asked him if there was any possibility of your application for entry into the electrical branch being considered.
It appeared to Captain Grant that you w-ere somewhat older than the average candidate, and he reports that he advised you that it was doubtful whether your application w-ould be considered and that in any ease there was then no time for an interview. You then asked if your racial origin would be a cause for rejection and Captain Grant informs me he replied that it might be but that, jn any event, final approval or rejection of a candidate is made by Naval Service Headquarters.
It is perhaps unnecessary for me to say that in voicing the view that your racial origin might be a cause for rejection Captain Grant was merely expressing his own personal opinion and in no way reflecting the policy of the Department. He was quite correct in stating that applications must be made to Naval Service Headquarters and that the final approval or rejection of any candidate must be made here.
If you desire to make application to the Naval Secretary, Naval Service Headquarters, Ottawa, for entry into the Royal Canadian Navy, I wish personally to assure you that your application will receive every consideration.
Yours very truly,
(Signed) D. C. Abbott.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE ON RESOLUTION PRECEDING MONET BILL
speechtext:
As announced last night, the first order for to-day is the consideration of the resolution respecting the loan to the United Kingdom. Before the item is called I feel that I should like to say a few words to hon. members about the procedure in debate on a resolution preceding a money bill. My reason for doing so is that the house having departed from its rules on some occasions during the last few years, the debates have been much longer than they otherwise would have been, and the public business has been delayed as a result. What I wish to say is that the rule is that a resolution must precede a money bill, but the resolution is intended merely as a notice to the house that a money bill is about to be introduced. It is not intended that the notice should be debatable; rather, the correct practice is that the resolution should be allowed to pass, the house go into committee and that, in committee, a statement be made on essential features of the bill which is later to be introduced, this to be followed if so desired by some brief discussion. It is not intended that a lengthy discussion should take place at that stage. The discussion on the bill should come after the bill itself is introduced.
I have spoken of this in previous sessions; if I recall aright, in 1943, when I think the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) who was then leading the opposition, agreed with me, at least in part, that it was desirable that discussion at the resolution stage should not be prolonged unduly: In 1944 I again drew the attention of the house to the position of a resolution preceding the introduction of a money bill. I again pointed out what I have said a moment or two ago. In that year, if I am not mistaken, the leader of the C.C.F. party expressed agreement with that view. Last year I was absent from the country at the time the resolution on the appropriation bill was before the house and I did not, therefore, speak of this particular aspect at the time, but I did notice that, by not following the rules, a very long debate took place in committee on the resolution. In fact, this is
what also occurred on the war appropriations bills in the other years I have referred to, with the result that, after weeks of discussion in committee on the resolution, the bill was introduced, and then the bill itself-I have forgotten whether this was the case last year or not, but I know it was the case in some years-went through with practically no discussion at all, but with some comment in the press thereafter that it seemed unwise for the house to be voting millions of dollars with little or no discussion on the second reading of the bill.
One of two things is certain to follow if we do not observe the rule; either the discussion which takes place on the resolution, and which may run along for days, may be repeated at great length in the debate on the bill, or, as I have just indicated, there will be a lengthy discussion on the resolution and then the house will take the view that, as the matter has already been discussed at length the bill itself should be allowed to go through with little or no discussion and, as a consequence thereof with some misunderstanding thereafter on the part of the public.
This morning, in order that I might give the house an official w-ord, I took up this matter with the Clerk. I have from him" a statement which I shall read as authoritative in the matter. It is as follows:
The motion for referring money resolutions to the committee of the whole is similar to the first reading of a bill which is not debatable under our standing order 71. The object of the resolution recommended by the crown is to give the house a first opportunity to decide if there is a prima facie case for introduction of a bill. The details of the projected measure are not then disclosed and the resolution is necessarily short although care is always taken that the terms used are sufficiently wide to cover the whole of the bill which will be subsequently introduced.
This house confirmed on June 1, 1936. the Speaker's decision to the effect that the fundamental terms of the resolution submitted to the house with the governor general's recommendation cannot be amended. In the United Kingdom parliament, where the standing order governing the case is the same as ours, no motion is made for the Speaker to leave the Chair when the order is called. May says, page 506:
"If a resolution appears on the notice paper to be considered in committee of the whole house under this standing order, and a minister of the crown signifies the royal recommendation, the Speaker leaves the Chair forthwith and the house resloves itself into committee."
As hon. members know, the Clerk has been a long time in the house and has followed its proceedings closely. Moreover he is an authority on the rules. He adds this paragraph:

When Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir Robert Borden led political parties in this house either on the treasury benches or in opposition they always took a firm stand against the discussion of a money resolution when the Speaker was in the chair. Their contention was that the motion was formal, and was only made because there was no other way for the house to go into committee of the whole.
As hon. members are aware, a committee of the house is considering the rules, and considering them with a view to making the proceedings somewhat less lengthy than they have been at times. I should think the best way to further the object we had in appointing that committee is to abide by such rules as we have already, and make such further amendments to them as may be necessary.
I am only explaining the situation to the house: I am sure what I have suggested is the correct practice, arid that, if followed, it will preserve all that the house may wish to preserve of the rights of members and will help materially to expedite its business.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, on a point of order: there are two things to consider. There is the motion that you put for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole, and there is the discussion of the resolution in the committee. If we do not discuss the motion when the chair puts it to the house, there is nothing in our rules which prevents a member from discussing the matter when the chairman of the committee of the whole is in the chair. These are two entirely different matters. The leader of the house knows that very well. But I just bring to the attention of hon. members the necessary distinction between both "discussions-the debate before Mr. Speaker, before the full house; and the discussion when the chairman or the deputy speaker is in the chair in committee of the whole.

speechtext:
As I understand it, there
can be the fullest discussion in committee; indeed the committee is the proper place for a discussion of details of a measure such as this. In order to introduce the discussion and the details it will be necessary for me to say something about the agreement itself and the principles underlying it, together with the reasons for it.
The financial agreement between the government of Canada and the government of the United Kingdom, signed on March 6th, was made public immediately after its signature and was made available to the members of fhe house in printed form at the beginning
of the session. In moving this resolution, I wish to explain as briefly as I can the essential purpose of the agreement as a whole and its various provisions.
This agreement is the keystone in the financial measures and arrangements made by this country for international trade and reconstruction.
The need for a credit of this magnitude and on these terms springs not only from the effects of the war upon Britain, but also from the vital importance to Canada of the re-establishment, expansion and continued development of foreign trade. As compared with others, Canadians enjoy a high standard of living. We look forward to a higher standard. We are making our plans to achieve that higher standard, but our country is so specialized in its resources and its development that it can provide high standards of living only by trade and exchange. Cut off from trade or faced with a severe loss of markets abroad, we could not maintain even our present standards, despite whatever success we might have in securing full employment. Given access to expanding foreign markets and to imports of things we require, we can make our own employment effective in yielding us living standards far beyond any that the average Canadian enjoyed before the war. Exporting the products of our farms, forests, mines and factories, utilizing cheap hydro power, Canadians can earn a living second only to that enjoyed by our neighbours in the United States. Denied the opportunity of exporting and importing on a large scale, however, we would become increasingly conscious that we are a small, northern country, lacking many of the resources and advantages which are necessary if a country is to live well within itself.
In normal times our employment, as well as our living standards, depends upon trade. When our export markets are depressed, Canadians are thrown out of work. Without a revival in exports, work can be found for them only on less productive jobs than those in the export trades. Our farmers and our other primary producers are vitally dependent upon foreign markets. The prices they receive and the amount which they can sell must, over the long run, be determined mainly by the markets outside- of Canada for our wheat, our bacon, our cheese, our apples, our fish, our lumber and our metals. In the short run we can give some protection to our farmers and our fishermen by floor prices and other such artificial devices; over the long run, however, nothing can protect their real interests against a loss of markets abroad.
Loan to United Kingdom

Our financial strength, as well as our economic prosperity, now requires high levels of national income, and therefore of foreign trade, to maintain the level of Government revenues that are required if the Government is going to meet all the commitments which have been undertaken, both as a result of the war and as a result of the changing views of the Canadian public on the responsibilities that any government should assume in conditions of to-day. If we are to be successful in our public finance, we cannot afford to be hesitant and half-hearted in promoting the foreign trade which is the basis of our prosperity.
Our interest is not simply in finding some place to put our surpluses; we must receive payment for our exports that can be used in discharging our own debts and in purchasing the imports which we require, and which we want for our higher standard of living. To accomplish this purpose we must be able to use the proceeds of our exports to the United Kingdom and the continent of Europe in paying our own bills and debts in the United States and in making purchases wherever we can best obtain the goods we need. We have a special interest in being able to use the currency that we receive for our exports, to obtain other currencies that we need for the payments we must make.
Already the government, with the support of parliament, has undertaken many measures to restore, expand and develop Canada's trade. The principal one to which I shall refer at
present is our programme of export credits, which is serving to finance a large part of our current exports. In the last session of parliament, on December 3, I made a detailed statement on our policies and operations in this field, and I shall not repeat here the substance of what I said at that time. As the leader of the opposition and others have asked me to review our foreign lending operations at this time, however, I wish to give the house a brief summary of the position up to the present.
Under part II of the Export Credits Insurance Act, as amended at the last session of parliament, our total authority for making direct loans to other governments is $750 million and our authority for giving guarantees is $200 million-and by that I mean I think it is two or three million dollars, or something like that-and no guarantees have been given since my review in December. Against our $750 million authority for direct loans we have now entered into agreements to lend $502,500,000. including the agreement with the government of France which was signed this week, and we have undertaken to lend additional amounts of $142,000,000 to those with whom we have already made agreements. This makes our total commitment $644,500,000 at present. Of this an amount of $67,412,051 had actually been advanced up to March 31.

During the latter part of 1945. In respect of some of the items it was agreed that it should be extended long before that. But there are so many transactions- some dealing with wheat, some with industrial equipment, and some with mutual aid supplies which were not delivered before the end of the war-that it is almost impossible to give a summary explanation in a few words.
So the total of the amount of credits covered by the agreements is $502,500,000; the amount of cash used up to March 31, 1946, is ,$67,412,051. Additional amounts committed for, which I have mentioned, amount to $142 million, making a total commitment of $644,500,000.
Then, as I started to say, for the sake of completeness, I should also mention that temporary advances have been made on behalf of allied governments under section 3 of the War Expenditure and Demobilization Appropriation Acts and previous War Appropriation Acts. During the past year these have served as temporary loans to certain of the governments to whom we are providing credits under The Export. Credits Insurance Act. A table of these advances as of February 28 was given in answer to a question and appears on page 417 of Hansard. It has not been possible to provide a complete table as yet for the same items as of March 31, as a number of the accounting transactions are not yet completed. I should mention, however, that the list for the end of March includes amounts of approximately $80 million on behalf of France, which will be repaid shortly from the export credit which has just been provided to that country, approximately $30 million on behalf of the United Kingdom, representing costs incurred subsequent to February 28 and therefore not covered by the claims agreement, approximately $14 million for the Netherlands, $9 million for the U.S.S.R., $8 million for Australia, and $5 million for Belgium. These figures do not include the items that have been settled by the claims agreement with the
United Kingdom, nor do they include certain expenditures made out of appropriated funds which it is expected to recover in whole or in part from other countries, such as military relief, for example, and costs of production of some supplies originally ordered for Mutual Aid and which are now being sold.
A detailed report on operations under part II of the Export Credits Insurance Act will be presented to the house later this month, and the house will have an opportunity to discuss them, as it is planned to bring into the house a bill amending certain provisions of that act, although not altering the amount that may be loaned under it.
Turning now to the special case of Britain, we should note first that her need for credits is huge in comparison with the other countries with which we have dealt.. Moreover, there are special factors in the case of the United Kingdom, which I shall discuss in a moment, that necessitate and justify different terms from those we have offered as a matter of policy in other cases. The government is, therefore, not proposing to deal with the credit to the United Kingdom under the Export Credits Insurance Act, but instead is seeking the specific approval of parliament for this financial agreement that has been concluded with the British government.
During the five years from 1946 to 1950, the United Kingdom will be going through a jjeriod of transition and reconstruction, both in its domestic and in its international economic affairs. In this period it will be endeavouring to revive and establish its export trade, which was so seriously curtailed during the war when all Britain's manpower was mobilized for war service, war production and only the most essential civilian purposes. It will take time for British exports to get back to their pre-war volume, although the progress made over the past few months is encouraging. It is necessary for Britain to do much more than to regain the pre-war levels, however, if she is to pay her way internationally. She has had to sacrifice many of the overseas investments she had made, and will no longer be able to count on as much income from this source as before to help her pay for imports.-This must be replaced by increased exports. Moreover, the losses incurred in shipping during the war have reduced, at least temporarily, the income from her merchant marine, while the general dislocation of trade and finance caused by the war has interfered with the British overseas earnings in respect of insurance and financing services, which also helped to pay for imports.
Loan to United. Kingdom

Loan to United Kingdom
These reasons for regarding. the United Kingdom position as a special one requiring special treatment are much more important in relation to>
Canada even than they are to the United States. They are more important for two reasons: first, because we are so much more vitally interested in the future of international trade as a whole than the United States, and, secondly, because such a large proportion of our trade takes place with the United Kingdom and other countries in the sterling area and we are most concerned to continue this trade and to continue to be able to receive payment for our exports to Britain and other sterling area countries in a form that we can use for expenditures elsewhere.
Britain has for many, many years occupied a key position in international trade and in its development. For more than a century it has been the greatest importing nation in the world. Despite the enormous growth of the importance of the United States in international trade and finance after the first world war, Britain remained much the largest importer. In 1938, for example, British imports comprised approximately 19 per cent of the total imports of the world, whereas American imports amounted to only slightly over eight per cent of the total. Nor do these figures alone make clear the great importance of Britain's markets. The nature of her1 imports was such that she constituted the chief market for countries such as Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Argentina and Denmark, as well as many smaller countries, all of which were greatly dependent upon exports for their prosperity and their general welfare.
Because of this large and central place which Britain occupies in world trade, British policies in regard to trade are of critical importance to exporting countries and particularly to Canada. In addition, British policies will influence and largely determine the policies of many other countries, including particularly the countries now in the sterling area and probably the countries of western Europe. If Britain follows one type of policy it will enable and encourage these other countries to follow it as well. Therefore, British trade policy in the next few years, when the whole pattern of postwar trade is to be determined, will be of the very greatest importance.
There are, broadly speaking, two alternative types of policy open to Britain at the present time. The first and much the more desirable policy from our point of view is the type reflected in the Bretton Woods agreements and the proposals for expansion of world trade and employment put forward by the United
States government. This type of trade and exchange policy involves a minimum of restrictions on trade, tariff reductions, the elimination of discriminatory import quotas and exchange practices, and the freedom of each country to use any currency that it has obtained through trade with another country in carrying on trade with any third country. This type of policy would make possible not only a high level of trade but freedom in the direction of trade. The alternative type of policy, on the other hand, which is open to the United Kingdom is one of bilateral arrangements in which Britain would purchase goods on condition that the selling country would take British goods in exchange, one involving discrimination in both importing and exporting and substantial restrictions on the use of currency received by exporting countries. Under this type of policy if Britain were forced to follow it, she would endeavour to make the most of the bargaining power which her huge import markets give her in order to improve the terms on which she trades and to force her exports into the markets of other countries.
The choice which Britain makes between these two alternative policies is vitally important to Canada as well as to the United States and to other countries which are largely dependent upon exports. There are many in the United Kingdom, some of them in very influential positions, who contend that Britain cannot afford the risks of liberal policies under present circumstances. They propose that she should exploit the strong bargaining position that will be hers after the present shortages disappear and buyers' markets return. Some persons in Britain even seem to see virtues in the political and economical arrangements likely to result from the restricted trading blocs which would emerge from a policy of bi-lateral bargaining and discrimination. On the other hand, there are many who realize, as we realize here, the advantages to Britain of liberal policies that will encourage the maximum development of trade. Britain can follow these policies which we favour if the British government and the British people can have confidence that they will possess sufficient financial resources to engage in trade on these liberal lines, which would involve more imports and a larger temporary increase in Britain's indebtedness than would the other policies, pending a revival in British export trade.
Britain cannot afford to choose the liberal trade policy' unless she gets loans from the United States and Canada on liberal terms. If she follows these policies, which we wish to see her adopt, she will have to discard
Loan to United Kingdom

within the next year many of the defensive and discriminatory import and exchange measures which she adopted during the war to protect her financial position under the enormous strains which the war thrust upon it. She will have to go into debt to the United States and to Canada, and perhaps to others, on a large scale. Britain can only afford to undertake these debts with any confidence of being able to repay them if the terms recognize the realities of her international financial position and make allowance for the relatively narrow margin she will have available over the long run to make repayment and pay interest. This necessity for liberal terms arises on the one side from the huge amounts which it is necessary for Britain to borrow, and on the other from the effects which the war has had upon her international financial position.
We must realize that Britain is no longer a wealthy country in international terms. She has sacrificed her international financial strength in meeting the costs of the war. Before the war Britain had substantial overseas assets that yielded her, on balance, an income of approximately a billion dollars a y'ear.
After Dunkirk, Britain, as part of her allout mobilization, threw all of her financial resources at home and overseas into the struggle, and used her ability to borrow abroad both in North America and in the sterling area. From that time until the end of hostilities, 3he incurred heavy costs outside her own borders in buying supplies and in financing the conduct of warfare in many parts of the world. The United States and Canada relieved her quite rightly of a considerable part of these costs in North America by' lend-lease and mutual aid. These, however, were truly part of our North American war effort rather than aid to Britain, who continued to carry more than her full share of the financial costs of the war. As a consequence of these huge overseas expenditures, Britain was forced to liquidate her overseas investments to. a value equivalent to approximately five billion Canadian dollars. About twenty per cent of these liquidated investments were Canadian securities. This liquidation of assets, however, was only the beginning. Britain proceeded to borrow heavily abroad in order to finance the costs of the war outside Britain and her total external debts increased by 'the equivalent of 13 billion Canadian dollars. In addition, she used up practically all her foreign exchange reserves before lend-lease commenced, and has only been able to rebuild them to little more than about half of what they were prior to Munich. As a consequence of all 
these changes, the British are now worse off to the extent of about 20 billion Canadian dollars than they were when the war commenced. Now the war and the effects of the war upon her exports and her overseas expenditure have left Britain in the situation where she must borrow a further five or six billion dollars during the transition period. As a result of the war, therefore, she will end up with her international position worsened by the equivalent of over twenty-five billion Canadian dollars, as compared with her position in 1939.
In addition to these losses in her external position, Britain of course suffered great losses at home-losses in property, in manpower and in wealth. We are all familiar with the spectacular damage caused by bombs and rockets; we are not so familiar with the insidious losses that arose because Britain was unable to repair and maintain her equipment, her houses and all the property that goes to make possible modern civilization. In addition, of course, the British cut down their standards of living and their consumption substantially below pre-war figures on average, while we on this continent were able to raise ours. I mention these losses within Britain only in order that we shall not seem to concentrate solely on the financial side. Other allies have suffered enormous losses in their own countries. None, however, has borne the international costs that Britain has borne; none is faced with the same tremendous problem of readjustment in the balance of their international payments. Alone among the allies, Britain has suffered as a result of the war a great deterioration in her external financial position and now, in addition, she must borrow huge new sums in order to embark in peacetime upon the trade policies which are so important to us.
The government has examined the present and prospective financial situation of Britain at length. We have come to the conclusion that Britain can undertake the trade and financial policies that she would like to undertake, and that we would like to see her undertake, if we and the United States are prepared to enter into financial agreements such as those already signed with her. We have come to the conclusion., after the most serious study and discussion of the matter, that terms more onerous than those provided in this agreement would not enable Britain to follow the policies which are in the long-run interests of both countries, and indeed of all countries. We have also come to the conclusion that the British government will be able to meet the terms of this agreement over the next fifty-five years. The British authorities themselves considered

Loan to United Kingdom
this aspeet of the matter most thoroughly and they have taken the most careful and responsible attitude possible in regard to the obligations which they have incurred under this agreement and the Anglo-American agreement. They have been determined from the outset, and indeed they made this determination clear to us as early as 1944, that they would not incur debts which they could not honestly believe they would be able to discharge.
I should like now to outline the main provisions of the agreement and to make some comments upon them that may help the house to understand their meaning and purpose.
In the first place, I should like to explain that this financial agreement and the other agreement on the settlement of war claims are separate and distinct. The agreement on the settlement of war claims is essentially a measure to settle with precision and finality a large number of outstanding claims between the two governments, without making any concession of consequence on either side. The amounts of some of the claims which are settled by this claims agreement are open to argument, and it would have been possible to spend years in debating whether this claim or that should be one or two or three million dollars, more or less, all things considered. Both sides have come to the conclusion that the payment by the United Kingdom to Canada of $150 million would be a fair and reasonable settlement of the net balance of the claims by Canada on the United Kingdom over the claims by the United Kingdom on Canada. There should, during the consideration of the estimates, be an opportunity for discussing the details of the claims covered by this agreement, if members wish to do so. The transactions to implement the agreement are being carried out under the War Expenditures and Demobilization Appropriation Acts of the 1945-46 fiscal year. Britain has already paid us in gold the $150 million she undertook to pay in this settlement.
The first item of interest in the financial agreement itself is, of course, the amount of the credit and the way in which it may be drawn upon. The British representatives asked for this amount, and demonstrated to our satisfaction that they would1 in fact require this much and more to finance the purchases which they intended to make in Canada during the six-year period in which the credit may be drawn upon. In fact, as I have already indicated, the British deficit of Canadian dollars will likely be such that the total amount of this credit will be drawn before the end1 of 1948. The British representatives made it clear 63260-49
to us that they expected that Britain would need to finance additional purchases ini Canada from other cash resources.
The terms of the loan relating to interest and repayment are, of course, the same as those in the agreement between Britain and the United States. During the years 1946-50 no interest is payable on the amount of the loan which will have been used. The reason for this is that this is the period during which Britain will be experiencing difficulty in her balance of payments as a result of the immediate after-effects of the war. This is the period during which she needs to use the credit, and she cannot afford to pay interest in this period without making additional credits necessary. Interest commences at the beginning of the year 1951 and for that year is payable on the whole amount outstanding at the end of the year. From that time on, interest is payable each year on the amount of the credit outstanding during that year. Principal repayments are made at the end of each year from 1951 to 2000 A.D.
We would naturally have preferred a higher rate of interest but after careful consideration of the probable British balance of payments, we reached the conclusion that two per cent was all that Britain would be in a position to pay. Indeed, she will not be able to afford even this rate of interest unless her exports expand and are maintained at-a high level. It is for this reason that waiver of interest payments is provided for under certain circumstances in our agreement as in the agreement with the United States. This is needed to allow for the uncertainties and risks which the United Kingdom must face in reestablishing her export trade. Interest may be waived only if the United Kingdom's exports over the preceding five years are insufficient to pay for the pre-war volume of her imports, taking into account other current account transactions as well. In effect, therefore, we say to the United Kingdom: If your exports are sufficient to enable you to pay for a prewar volume of imports without running further into debt, then we will demand interest from you; if, however, they are not up to this level and if, therefore, you must go into debt or liquidate your capital in order to import on the pre-war scale, or else must restrict your imports to avoid the strain upon * your resources, then we are prepared to waive the interest payments.
I should point out that the waiver will only be granted if the United Kingdom states that it is necessary in view of the present and prospective conditions of international exchange and the level of her gold and foreign exchange reserves, and if the international monetary

fund certifies that the condition in respect of United Kingdom exports is fulfilled. We have also the safeguarding provision that the waiver will only be granted by Canada if it is also being granted by other countries having similar agreements, which, of course, include the United States and any further countries which may enter into agreements of this kind with the United Kingdom. This waiver clause should go a considerable distance in enabling us to avoid any possible damaging effects of the burden of large scale indebtedness upon future trade in the event of adverse economic circumstances.
The next important provision of the agreement is article 5 regarding exchange and import arrangements. It will be noted that this is reciprocal in form, and that each of the two governments agrees to accord to the other treatment not less favourable than that provided for in any instrument of agreement with the government of any other country, signed prior to the date of this agreement. Under this clause Canada binds herself to give the United Kingdom most-favoured-nation treatment in regard to the use of import quotas, which are referred to in some of our trade agreements. The United Kingdom, on the other hand, in this clause undertakes to give Canada similar treatment to that granted the United States in the Anglo-American financial agreement. This is of quite substantial importance. Hon. members will recall that there are 4 important sections of the Anglo-American agreement relating to these questions. Under certain of them the United Kingdom agrees to make sterling paid by the United Kingdom in current -account transactions, or sterling released from accumlated balances, freely convertible and available for current transactions in any currency area without discrimination. On the other hand, certain of the undertakings given in the Anglo-American agreement apply specifically to the treatment of United States transactions or trade, and it is the benefit of these provisions in particular that we obtain under Article 5 of our agreement. In particular, we obtain the benefits of paragraph (i) of section 8, in which the United Kingdom undertakes not to apply exchange control in such a manner as to restrict payments or transfers in respect of [DOT]current transactions between the two countries, or the use of sterling balances to the credit of residents of the United States arising out of current transactions. We also obtain the important benefits of section 9, in which the government of the United Kingdom agrees to administer any import restrictions on a basis which does not discriminate against imports from the other country in respect of any pro-
duct. This assurance of non-discrimination in import control is to take effect as soon as practicable, and not later than the end of 1946. We shall obtain the benefit of this nondiscrimination as a result of Article 5 of our agreement.
Article 6 of the agreement provides in effect that .the arrangements already existing in respect of the loan which we made to the United Kingdom in 1942 will continue as they are at present until the beginning of 1951, and that before that date we shall discuss the question of payment of interest on, and the , terms of repayment of, any balance of the loan then outstanding. Members will probably recall that this loan was made under the War Appropriation (United Kingdom Financing) Act, 1942. In substance, the actual loan was made to Britain to finance war expenditures during 1941, as we were providing Britain with dollars in 1941 in return for sterling which we accumulated and this accumulated sterling was paid off with the $700 million loan granted in 1942. The loan was, of course, a war loan, made to finance war expenditures. The act which authorized it provided that no interest shall be payable under such obligation in respect of any period prior to the termination of the war. Consequently the loan has not -borne interest up to date. In view of the enormous burden of international debt which war has thrust upon Britain and the difficulty she faces in reestablishing her export trade and paying for all her current requirements, we have come to the conclusion that Britain has not the capacity to pay interest on this loan during the period from now until the end of 1950, any more than on the main loan, and that she should not be asked to do so. There has been another important arrangement concerning this loan which is being continued under the new agreement. At the time we made this loan in 1942, the United Kingdom government undertook to ensure that the proceeds of sales to persons not resident in the United Kingdom of Canadian securities payable in Canadian currency, and interests therein, held by residents of the United Kingdom, and the proceeds of the redemption or repayment of Canadian securities or -interests therein held by residents of the United Kingdom were paid to the -government of Canada as part repayment of this loan. This arrangement is now being extended and will continue until the end of 1950, along with the interest-free provision. Under this arrangement the loan is being paid off or reduced by the sale or redemption of Canadian securities held in Britain. This process will result in the gradual and orderly repatriation of Canadian securities

owned in the United Kingdom, and in the gradual reduction of the amount of the loan outstanding. The total repayments up to date have amounted to §161,435,596.43. Additional repayments are pending as a result of the substantial sales and redemptions of securities in the latter part of 1945, and when they are made the loan will be reduced to something in the neighbourhood of $500 millions.
Article 7 of the agreement provides for the cancellation of the amount owing by the government of the United Kingdom to Canada under the British commonwealth air training plans of 193-9 and 1942. These agreements were the basic ones under which this great Canadian project, one of the most creditable aspects of our war record, was developed and financed. In broad terms, the agreements provided for the sharing of the total costs of these plans among Canada, Britain, Australia and New Zealand in proportions considered fair at the time in view of the number of pupils from the several countries to be trained under the plans, and also in view of other relevant circumstances at the time. Under both the first and second plan, the United Kingdom share was intended to be financed mainly through contributions in kind, that is, contributions of aircraft, spares, supplies and equipment. As the plans developed and as the various circumstances affecting the ability of the United Kingdom to make contributions in kind changed, for example, when the great intensification of the air war in 1940 made it difficult for the United Kingdom to send planes to Canada for training purposes, the share of the United Kingdom in the total costs came considerably to exceed the amount which she could furnish as contributions in kind. As a consequence, when the settlement of the accounts for the first plan was finally worked out, it was found that the United Kingdom's share of the cost exceeded what she had contributed and paid by $200 million. Similarly, when the details for the second plan, ending at March 31, 1945, were worked out, it was found that the United Kingdom had paid or contributed an amount that fell short of her share of the costs by $225 million. These two sums together add up to the $425 million referred to in this financial agreement. The detailed methods by which the shares of costs were determined, and the various items credited to the United Kingdom are exceedingly complicated, and if the house wishes to know more about them when considering the bill, I am sure that the Minister of National Defence for Air, with some advance notice, would be able to give an explanation of them.

In agreeing to cancel this amount owing by Britain in respect of air training, the government has been motivated by a number of strong reasons. In the first place, this service provided to Britain is one that might well have been covered by mutual aid, and perhaps would have been covered by mutual aid had not the air training agreements been entered into before mutual aid began and the accounts worked out only after, mutual aid had terminated. We did provide air training services to Australia and New Zealand as mutual aid, and we furnished supplies to Britain as mutual aid that could be used for air training in Britain. Secondly, the United States government furnished air training services to Britain and to other countries as lend-lease and furnished Britain with equipment and supplies on a large scale to be used in air training, including equipment and supplies used in the British Commonwealth air training plan in Canada. Thirdly, we came to the conclusion after much consideration that repayment of this $425 million was beyond the United Kingdom's capacity to pay within any reasonable period. From what I have already . said, it will be evident that the amount which the British can undertake to pay is severely limited within the next five years and, indeed, over the remainder of this century. We have taken full account of their ability to pay in setting the terms for interest and repayment on the new loan and for the 1942 loan. It seems to us futile to ask the British government to pay this $425 million some time in the next century when they have completed the payments on the loan which we are now making to them. I do not believe that either the British or the Canadian people at that time would consider it a proper transaction. I think it is far better for us to face the facts clearly and cancel this particular war debt. It should be remembered that the British have no production assets as a result of incurring this debt-nothing that will add to their ability to pay it.
I need say only a few words about the remaining articles of the agreement. Article 8 regarding consultation indicates that the two governments will work together in putting the agreement into effect, and that if major changes -occur in the international situation which materially alter the prospective benefits and obligations flowing from the agreement, they will consider together what changes in its provisions they should agree to make, subject to such legislative approval as may be necessary. By consultation we shall be able to work out such things as the manner and

I should now refer to the exchange of notes between the Chancellor of the Exchequer and myself in regard to our understanding about the entering into force and implementation of the various provisions of the agreement. This was made necessary because the agreement has been drawn up in the expectation that the financial agreement between the United Kingdom and the United States, signed at Washington on December 6 last, will be approved by the American congress and will entet into force some time during the current year. As soon as that agreement does enter into, force, we shall be prepared to implement the whole of our agreement once parliament has approved it. If, however, congress does not approve the Anglo-American agreement, we shall consider that, in the terms of article S of our agreement, a major change has occurred in the international financial situation which would materially alter the prospective benefits and obligations flowing from our agreement, and that consequently it would be necessary forthwith to consider what changes in the provisions of our agreement the governments of Canada and the United Kingdom should agree to make, subject to such legislative approval as may be necessary, which, of course, in our case would be approval by parliament in the event of any amendment to the agreement itself. If congress does not approve the Anglo-American agreement, we shall not benefit from the trade and exchange provisions of that agreement, either directly or through the application of article 5 of our agreement. It will, therefore, be necessary to consider some substitute for article 5 of our agreement in those circumstances. Consequently we feel that those portions of our agreement which it is not necessary to implement immediately in order to enable the United Kingdom to proceed now with its purchases in Canada should be deferred until we see the results of congressional action. For that reason, therefore, we have reached the understanding with the United Kingdom that articles 5, 6 and 7 of the agreement will not be implemented until it is known whether the United1 States congress has approved the Anglo-American agreement.
In conclusion Mr. Chairman I wish to say ju&t this. The United Kingdom has always been Canada's largest and most reliable market. Upon the continuation of this market the employment and welfare of millions of Canadians depend. It must cease to be a satisfactory market for Canadian products unless the British pound is in the future both convertible and stable. The restoration of the
[Mr. Ilsley.l
convertibility of sterling and the maintenance of a reasonable stability of sterling depend upon the successful completion of the proposed loan agreements with the United States and Canada. If these go through, Great Britain can take her full part in the post-war period and throughout the years of the future as a great trading nation, a nation whose currency can be used by any country to buy the products of any other country; a nation whose currency will retain a stable value from year to year. Viewed in this light, this agreement is of the highest importance, and value to Canada. It is not in any sense an act of charity, it is an investment in the future of Canadian trade. Together with the Anglo-American agreement and the Bretton Woods agreements, it will enable us to proceed confidently to the consideration of the commercial policy that Canada and other countries should follow after the war, and to the establishment of the international trade organization which has been proposed by the United States. As hon. members already know, it is planned to have an international conference on trade and employment some time within the next twelve months. Preceding that will be a smaller conference, sponsored by the economic and social council of UNO, for the purpose of drawing up specific proposals for the consideration of the larger conference and, more particularly, foy the negotiation of specific proposals for the reduction of tariffs. These measures, relating to international trade and the barriers to such trade, are of the utmost importance to Canada. We can proceed to a proper consideration of them and to the action that will be based upon such consideration only if the financial resources that will make trade possible are provided by agreements such as that which has been placed before the committee .for approval.

I suppose it is no exaggeration to say that what we do in this house at the present time may have an influ-

ence far beyond ourselves. What we are being asked to do, as the Minister of Finance has pointed out, is to take part in what may be described as a piece of global economic strategy. We heard a great deal about global strategy during the war, and I take it we must have global strategy to-day, in times of peace, when we face questions just as difficult as we faced in the war, if not more so. and in an atmosphere more difficult because we have not now that inspiration, urgency and common feeling which come from sharing a common danger which we can feel day by day in terms of human life. I believe we are facing just as great a common danger to-day, but it is not so easy to see it.
I wish to discuss this matter solely from the point of view of the economic interest of Canada. That is not because I have not any other feeling about the matter. I might speak from other points of view, but the reason I wish to speak from that point of view is that I want to put it on a basis where no Canadian fellow citizen can say to me, "you have introduced an extraneous element here." I want to put it on a basis where I can say to any Canadian citizen. "I am arguing this from the point of view of your interest and my interest, our Canadian interest, our economic interest." I have some hope that if we can all make each other believe that we are really arguing it on that basis and that there is nothing else in it, we can reach that measure of unanimity which I regard as very important.
The next observation I wish to make is that I believe every one in this house-I really said this already-realizes the enormous, the vital importance of this. If this succeeds 

if we have faith we can make it succeed- we have a chance to go forward to some kind of economic cooperation comparable with what we had during the war. If we ourselves, the United States and the United Kingdom reach some kind of coordination and cooperation the rest of the world will, I am sure, be glad to follow. If we fail, then there is literally no hope for anything except the old chaos which we all got to know so well in the thirties.
I come to the bill, the first section of which says that the government of Canada will extend to the government of the United Kingdom a credit of SI ,250,000,000. What do we mean by that? What does that mean in terms of the life of the ordinary Canadian citizen? We have become so accustomed to these fabulous and ast-onomical amounts that we are getting to feel they are just figures in books, and some .people tell us that they are
just figures in books. I should like to describe what it means to me in as simple words as I can. What it means is that the citizens of Canada are to be asked either to pay taxes or to lend money to that amount, to make that amount available to the people of Great Britain and of other places, as the Minister of Finance pointed out, to buy goods in this country. Why do we do that? Do we do that just to make ourselves good fellows, because we are generous-hearted? No. Why do we do it? All hon. members know why we do it. I ventured to say last autumn when the exports credits were up that we could not afford not to afford them. I say the same thing about this amount. Why do I say that? What do I mean when I say it? All hon. members need to do is to look back over the last fifteen years. They do not need to go another step backward to see what foreign trade means in the life of this country. We remember the figures of 1929. Our exports amounted to something like $1,400 million. Then it went down in 1933 to little more than one-third of that amount. I believe it was S534 million. We all know what that meant. Then by uncertain, rather anxious and slow degrees it mounted up in 1939 until it was something over $900 million, just under a billion, if I remember rightly. We all know what happened since that time. It mounted up and up until it got to about $5 billion. We know how that happened. We know that we borrowed, that we taxed ourselves as we never believed we could. The Minister of Finance almost made us like it. We taxed ourselves to the extent of about two and a half billion dollars, and on top of that we borrowed almost another two and a half billion dollars. In various other ways the minister managed to raise about another $500 million. Altogether we took out of our pockets about S5.500 million. The result was we were all rich. We all had money in our pockets. There is great danger lest we feel somehow or another that these good times with these fabulous amounts can just go on. The truth of the matter is that we are like a man who had an income of $2,500 and then borrowed $2,500 and spent the whole $5,000 in one year and said, "This is grand", and did not bother very much about what is to come afterwards.
The Minister of Finance smiles. He knows better than that, and we are going to know better when we look at it. The longer the spree, the sorer our heads will be when we wake up. I do not think many of us believe there is some magic which enables us to go on borrowing and borrowing and never have to pay the piper. Incidentally I am glad that

I do not like to think of what would happen, first of all to Europe, and then to us, if Britain is not able to restore her economy. Therefore it seems to me that when we are talking about assisting her to restore her economy we are talking about something which is very close to ourselves. I should like to read a few words from a speech of Lord Keynes which was delivered in the British House of Commons. He was speaking about his trip to the United States and the negotiations that were carried on last autumn. He referred to the attitude which they had to take in the United States. He was answering some people in Britain who felt, I suppose naturally, that since they had been in the war for two and a quarter years before the United States there might have been a somewhat different attitude taken toward all the amounts which were spent, and spent in the United States, during those two and a quarter years. But Keynes told them to forget all about that, and he had one or two important remarks to make on it, I should like to read one or two of them. It is, I think, put in rather clever wording. This is what he said:
We soon discovered that it was not our past performance or our present weakness, but our future prospects of recovery and our intention to face the world boldly that we had to demonstrate.

He went on to say:
In every circle in which I moved during my stay in Washington, it was when I was able to enlarge on the strength of our future competitive position, if only we were allowed a breather, that I won most sympathy.
Why do I read this to the house? I do so for two reasons: first of all, to try to underline the argument that I am making. If I succeed in nothing else I hope I shall succeed in showing that I am arguing this from the point of view of the interest of Canada. My second reason for reading it is to draw to the attention of the house what Mr. Keynes said, who, I suppose, on his record of the last twenty-five years can clearly be regarded not only as the greatest economist, but the most successful prophet that we have had in economic matters. In case I forget later, I should like to remind the house of that astounding book he wrote in- 1919 called "The Economic Consequences of the -Peace," in which he repeated everything that has happened since; at any rate, everything that has happened with respect to the indemnities of the first war. He said they could not be paid-. Keynes pointed out the whole thing. Here is the man who was in Washington. Here is the man who told- the British that in dealing with the United States they had to satisfy the people of that country that they would- be able to recover; that this global strategy of economics would succeed, that if they were given this breathing space they could get on their feet and be able to fit again into a freer world1 economy, and that this would- be to the advantage of the United States and ourselves.
Let us remember when we are talking about this that the negotiations in the United States-and Keynes pointed this out in the British House of Commons-were always carried out with congress in mind. There was 'congress; and congress was considered to be representative chiefly of the people of the middle west. In other words, they wanted to get down to hard-boiled people who considered nothing about sentiment, but who were looking to their own advantage.
To me the matter is very simple. I shall give a simple illustration drawn from business. I do not know if I have used it before in the house; but if you have escaped it, there are a lot of other people who have not. It is this: We all know that in business, the wise businessman very often finds it necessary to give credit. The wholesaler may give credit to the retailer, and he may not pay for a year or two years, or even three or more. Why does the wholesaler give credit to the retailer? Does he do it because he likes the

retailer? Indeed not; he may dislike him. He does it because he thinks this man is a sound businessman, and he hopes to set up a good customer. That is why we should make this loan to Great Britain.
I wish now to say a word-and no more than a word, because the Minister of Finance has covered it, and I do not wish to labour it-about another phase of the matter. It is well for us to remember two things that happened during the war. It is well for us to remember why these people need help. It is not because they are a lot of poor weaklings who have mismanaged their own affairs. It is not because of that at all. It is because they have fought a war for six years. It is because they had to take their savings for generations-perhaps centuries-and use them, as wre know, to buy astronomical amounts of supplies in the United States.
The , result is that that great source of income is just about cut in two. But that is not the worst. The worst is that after the United States came into the war, and when things seemed to be going better, when prospects were better, in the last years of the war Great Britain had to make this great distortion in her economy, namely, that she had practically to give up her foreign trade. She had to make the things that she could make at home, for use at home; and the United States and other countries took over the foreign trade. This was necessary to save shipping, and to prevent so far as possible the unnecessary use of shipping in submarine infested waters. The fact of the matter is that these unfortunate people, while fighting for their lives, saw their trade drop to about thirty per cent of what it was in 1939-and it was nothing to boast about even in 1939. That is, the reason why we a^e faced with this situation.
There are two alternatives, and, I think, only two. The first is that of multilateral trade, to which the Minister of Finance has referred, and which we hope will become real under this International Conference of Trade and Employment which is to meet during the current year.
What is it hoped that may do? It is hoped that may get us away from the multitudinous restrictions we have, and about which we all know so much. We would all like to get awray from them if we can. I do not think there is any doubt about that. It is a policy to free sterling currency, which at the present time is not free. They have had to stipulate in England that people who sell there have to leave their money in England, so that sterling could be used and marshalled and
the small amount of United States exchange could be kept in a pool, which was managed by Great Britain.
The whole aim of loans by the United States and ourselves is to set that free and, as the Minister of Finance said, so that money can be used freely throughout the world, so that we can get back to the method left behind, so that we can do business again without being hampered with all these numerous checks and balances.
What is the alternative? The alternative is a very simple one. I shall read again the words of Keynes, and I would ask hon. members to note carefully what he says. The alternative, of course, is to go on with the sterling bloc. The alternative is for Great Britain to seek more credits from the countries in the sterling block to whom she already owes a lot, particularly those in the sterling bloc who have not the goods that we in Canada and the United States have, and who have not the materials which are needed by the United Kingdom in order to get its business under way.
This is what Keynes said in the debate in the House of Lords:
The alternative is to build up a separate economic bloc which excludes Canada and consists of countries to which we already owe more than we can pay, on the basis of their agreeing to lend us money they have not got, and buy only from us and one another goods we are unable to supply.
May I read it again, because it is true. Perhaps it sounds like a clever epigram; but let me read it again:
The alternative is to build up a separate economic bloc which excludes Canada and consists of countries to which we already owe more than we can pay-
That is, each country in the sterling bloc.
-on the basis of their agreeing to lend us money that they have not got-
They have already extended credit beyond their means.
[DOT]-and buy only from us and one another goods we are unable to supply.
Because the people who can supply them are the United States and Canada.
I want now to come back to one observation he makes here which, to my mind, is vital, when, he says, "This economic bloc which excludes Canada." I believe there is an argument for Australia or New Zealand or South Africa, or France or Belgium. I think there is an argument in the case of these countries that they might flourish under a sterling bloc. But I cannot see how there is an argument that

we can flourish in it, because we cannot get into it. The reason for that is that nature has put us in North America. We are inescapably north American-as a distinguished leader of my party said about, ten years ago. We are inescapably, geographically north American.
If we are not in the sterling bloc, then will hon. members and will the people of this country please reflect upon what that means? As I said a minute ago, I believe every sensible man, if he could visualize these two alternatives, would not hesitate a moment as to which he would take. Again, if we can have multilateral trade, which means going back to the simple and sensible world-certainly it was sensible when compared with the mess we have been in since-of the nineties, or opening years of the present century. I do not mean that they were perfect; I do not mean that our social services were what they should be. I am thinking about the international situation and the likelihood that any sensible man would wish to go back to that reasonable degree of freedom.
