But if we could1 get back to those conditions, when there was a reasonable degree of freedom, trade moved1, goods moved freely, and people benefited from each other's capacity to specialize, as the minister pointed, out. That is what we should have again.
What reason have we to think that that may succeed? First, I would say-this may be a rather negative reason-that there are

a lot of people still in places of responsibility who know the terrible results of not doing it. They remember what happened in the 1930's. I was reading a book this morning which pointed out the awful effects of economic'nationalism running mad. It pointed out that in 1929 Germany, Italy and France imposed tariffs on wheat amounting to as much [DOT]as $1.83 a bushel. The result was that in the succeeding five years 600,000,000 bushels less wheat were imported into those countries than in the previous five. The competent writer of this book reckoned that that cut d6wn the purchasing power in this country by some $200 million per annum.
We remember these fantastic things and any sensible man wants to do everything possible to get away from them.
In the second place we have moved into a world where, although there are perhaps a lot of grandiloquent and more or less irresponsible things said about full employment, not only, public conscience but political necessity demand that the state shall never stand by again and see unemployment in a big way without using all the resources of the state to prevent it. We have this great hope, particularly when we look at the United States-if you have prosperity in the United States, then the thing will go. If you have prosperity in the United States you will have trig imports into the United States; if you have big imports into the United States, that is half the battle because that will get the wheel turning everywhere.
You have only to look back to see what happened to British exports in 1929, 1930 and 1931 when the United States went flat. British exports went down by fifty per cent. There you have it.
May I come back to Keynes; I do not want to be tiresome by quoting him but, after all, Keynes is considered, as I said a few minutes ago. to be a very great expert. He has been the best prophet on these matters that we have had and he has the great advantage of having lived last year for several months in the United States. He says:
All the most responsible people in the United States and particularly in the state department and the treasury, have entirely departed from the high tariff, export subsidy, conception of things, and will do their utmost with, they believe. the support of public opinion in the opposite direction. That is why this international trade convention presents us with such a tremendous opportunity. For the first time in modern history the United States is going to exert its full powerful influence in the direction of reduction of tariffs, not only of itself, but by all others.
I should like to give one little illustration culled from yesterday's press which shows the difficulty we are running into, because of

Loan to United Kingdom
the mixed-up world we havq now where the individual who is trying to do business finds himself cribbed, cabined and confined at every turn. I read in the New York Times an unfavourable reference to a stepchild of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), the Canadian Commercial Corporation. The New York Times takes a rather dark view of that, the minister will be glad to know. This article states that the operations of this corporation will be unfair in connection with ordinary trade movements, and it quotes one individual as follows:
The important thing, one exporter declared, "is not what the Canadian corporation is set up to do, but that it is set up at all."
I am not going to labour this, and incidentally I should point out that the report is quite fair because it gives the minister's explanation when it says:
According to the Canadian Minister of Trade and Commerce, the commercial corporation is intended to take over the various functions of making purchases in that country for foreign governments and LTNRRA; to assist private enterprise in obtaining essential supplies from former enemy territories, and to provide machinery to purchase sugar, tea, oils and fats, which are under international allocation or foreign government control.
I am not complaining about that; I am only mentioning it to show what a fantastic world we live in. This morning I talked to an exporter who had been groaning under these restrictions. He said, "We exporters are not a lot of dumbells; we are ready to do business, but when we want to we have to go to this board and we get wound round and round with red tape." Perhaps that is not a criticism of the board, because what else can it do? We all know that when you get a board and put a man at the head of it with a lot of people underneath him, the rest of them cannot assume any responsibility. Do not let us fool ourselves about what happens when you get a board like this. What you do is to set up a little kingdom-perhaps it will become a government secret and be forgotten by the cabinet. I understand that this board is presided over by an able and energetic man who got his training under the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe).
Probably a good Tory.

All the better if he is, except that if he is a good Tory he will be a man of energy who will want to do a good job, and doing a good job will mean doing a big job. Whoever this gentleman is, and I do not know his politics, no doubt he will be faithful to his minister. If that is so he will have a great desire to exercise power; he will have a great desire to push other 63260-50
people around. My feeling is that that board will go on and on acquiring more and more power, unless some strong person, unless the Minister of Trade and Commerce keeps his hand on it and prevents it from doing so. I am not joking; that is what happens when you put a man on a board who wants to do a job. When you have a man who thinks he can very easily make himself believe that he knows more about it than anyone else, especially when other people have to come and do double handsprings before him. He may begin to believe that all these business men know nothing at all and he will want to stay there as long as possible. That is the sort of thing we should be trying to get away from. That is the sort of thing we shall begin to get away from if this agreement, which permits a reasonable freedom of action, is carried.
I want to repeat myself just briefly and I promise not to say it all over again. There will be difficulties; there will be objections raised. Incidentally, I am only discussing the principle and I may be raising objections to certain details. The alternative which Keynes outlined is, to me, unthinkable. It is an alternative which leaves Canada, as I say, to be ground between the upper and nether millstones. I hope with all my heart that in this debate we shall be able to consider this matter from the point of view of the true economic interests of Canada. I believe that if it is rightly considered in that way there is only one answer.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to make any extended remarks this afternoon in connection with the statement that has been placed before us by the minister, except to say that I believe that the putting into effect of these agreements will be beneficial, not only to Canada but to the entire world. Therefore we are prepared to support this agreement, reserving to ourselves the right to make inquiry into details to understand it better. We should, not only in this house but throughout the country, consider agreements of this sort in a more realistic way.
It seems to me that all of us at times are under what I might call a money illusion. We think in terms of money and we think in terms of financial agreements and financial returns from those agreements. As a matter of fact, what we are actually doing is to send, in this case to the United Kingdom, certain goods which she requires and which she cannot herself produce. If we are to do the same thing for the other nations whose loans have been mentioned this afternoon, and these loans are to be repaid from 1946 to 1976 or from 1949 to 1979, as the case may be,

77S
Loan to United Kingdom

we shall if we are wise, if we have the ability to do so in spite of the contradictions of our present economic system, import into our country not pounds and shillings and pence or francs or any ot-her foreign currency, but quantities of goods which will enable us to raise our own standards of living. That is what agreements of this sort should mean. In this time of necessity we need to help rebuild the economy of the world and to assist our best customer to place herself once more in the position of being able to take from this country goods which she will ultimately repay in goods which we shall receive from her or from some other country obligated to make payments to her, and we should so arrange our affairs that we shall be able to take these goods and use them for improving our own standards of living.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), who has just made a very fine speech about the matter, said a few moments ago that during the war we taxed ourselves and borrowed from ourselves as we never taxed and borrowed before. But is it really true that we accomplished the miracles we accomplished during the war just by taxing and borrowing from ourselves as we never did before? That is not true. We accomplished those miracles by producing as we never produced before. Taxing and borrowing money? Money meant nothing at all during the war. It was the production of goods for the winning of the war that counted; because we produced as we never produced before we were able to accomplish the wonders we achieved during the war, and so long as we are able to maintain those high levels of production we can continue to perform miracles in supplying the nations with the goods which they need in order to recover their economy and at the same time help to raise our own standards of living in this country by improving the housing situation and supplying the various other things we ourselves need at the present time.
One of the difficulties is this. Never at any time have the producers of our country had the means to use the goods which they produced or the goods that are returned to us in exchange for the goods which we produce and export, and consequently the time comes when we find ourselves in the position of having to safeguard our economy, as it is called, and we endeavour to build a wall around ourselves. I was delighted to hear the hon. member from Muskoka-Ontario speak in the way he did this afternoon about opening up the channels of trade. That is indeed refreshing coming from the party with which

he is associated. But may I add that even to-day when I pick up articles or read speeches by friends of my hon. friend I see that they insist on the necessity of retaining the imperial preferences and the Ottawa agreements. Yet, if ever agreements were made that were restrictive of international commerce it was the Ottawa agreements.
*An hon. MEMBER: They made reductions.

There we have an interruption from the same party discounting the words used this afternoon by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. If we are to have a free flow of trade, we can never have it by building a wall around Canada or around the association of nations known as the British commonwealth, and one of the reasons why I am prepared to support these loan agreements is that they will tend to open up world trade.
I am not unmindful of the fact that these agreements, so far as Canada is concerned, can be successful only in so far as our great neighbour to the south follows intelligent international economic policies. Here I believe is the great danger, because the United States remains to-day an island of capitalism in a world that tends ever more to socialization or socialism, or whatever you like to call it. Those contradictions in the capitalist system in the United States will compel her in the long run to try to protect her own economy and her own standards, as she calls them, by keeping out goods from the rest of the world, with the result that we shall have deepening unemployment.
I did not want to introduce any discussion of the United Kingdom budget but my hon. friend asked if Mr. Dalton was a socialist. I have known Hugh Dalton for a long time and I would say he is a pretty thorough-going socialist in his thinking and in his views. Let me point out to my hon. friend that I shall be quite content if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) here in his first full year's budget after the war follows Mr. Dalton's example. Mr. Dalton has relieved entirely British income tax payers in the lower brackets to the number of two and a half million people, and if the Minister of Finance here will relieve our income tax payers in the lower brackets and restore the pre-war income tax exemptions in this country, that will be an instalment of income tax relief which we shall be very glad to welcome in this house.

speechtext:
Would the hon. member be content if I took the English exemptions and took the excess profits tax off?

No. My right hon. friend asks me if I am prepared to accept the English income tax exemptions and I answer no, because our economies and social services are so different and always have been.
Oh.

Yes. We are making loans to Britain at the present time. Do not forget that we are a rich country and that the British people are compelled to dig down deeper than we are. Nevertheless they have restored the pre-war level, at least of income tax exemptions, and yet we, a rich country, have not restored the pre-war levels. I say that if the Minister of Finance will do that in his 'budget we shall have a word of commendation for him. Let me point out, too, that the British have retained the super-taxes on high incomes; let us retain them too. They have increased their succession duties; let us increase them too. Then see how my hon. friends to my right will greet such a budget. It is true that the British budget provides that the excess profits tax will be removed at the end of the year, but it retains the war profits tax of five per cent. Let my hon. friends approve the taxation of profits too, and then we shall be more on common ground. It is no good to cite Britain as an example unless one states exactly what is happening there, and it is time we understood just exactly what they are doing to implement their policies.
In almost the same breath the hon. member made the statement that we dare not go back to the conditions of 1930. It is true that we dare not go back, but I believe that we are headed for those conditions under the policies now being put into effect in North America. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario says that if there is any tendency to go back to the conditions of 1930 we must use all the powers of the state to see that that does not happen. "Use all the powers of the state"? But we find my hon. friends demanding at the same time that controls shall be removed, that the powers of the state shall be curtailed. That would prevent us from doing the very thing he wants, using the power of the state to prevent a recurrence of the conditions of 1930. I find it very difficult to understand the logic of some of my hon. friends.
Do not blame that on the logic.

There is no logic in it. It sounds well, but when you pick up the speech and read it the day after, it will appear like a good many things that you have said the night before appear the day after.

So, Mr. Chairman, all I want to do is to say that when the proper occasion arrives we shall have more to say about this, but meantime I believe that the agreement entered into is, in the main, a good agreement and we are prepared to give it our support.

First of all may I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) on the excellent presentation which he has made. Since I have been here I do not think he has ever said anything in the house which I could so heartily support as the speech which he has just delivered. One of the main reasons why I can support so enthusiastically what he has said is that he is finally, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) points out, on a goods and services basis.
If I recall correctly, the minister did point out that it would be impossible for the British people to get their pound up to value and keep it stable unless they had this loan; and this loan is a loan of goods. It is the goods and services which a people can produce that make for the stability of their money. Once the whole world begins to see that, it will begin to look at this situation which so grieves the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), not as a completely bewildering and incomprehensible puzzle, but as a labyrinth from which there is a way out to be found.	[DOT]
I do not propose to discuss this matter at length because, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar points out, there will be plenty of opoprtunities to have much more to say as we go forward. But I should like to point out three matters which, in my judgment, ought to be borne in mind in dealing with this loan. I will discuss it briefly from three points of view: first of all, from the point of view of defence; second, from the point of view of good business; and third, from the point of view of common decency and national self-respect.
We are in a world of grim realities. In our own lives we have seen two wars. Who can say that we shall not yet in our own lives see a third war? Britain has saved us twice in the memory of those in this chamber. Who is to say that we shall not need to have Britain save us a third time?
Canada is a member-if one may use an athletic expression-of the British commonwealth and empire team. Thus far this team has won every series. The United States has thus far played in our team as a star, and Great Britain has also been a star player in the team. Great Britain has been seriously injured in the last series, and we must get
Loan to United Kingdom

her back into good condition; we must make her fighting fit again. Fighting strength in these days depends more and more upon fro-ductive capacity, economic strength and financial strength. If, then, we are to restore Great Britain to a condition of fighting fitness we must restore her economically and financially.
Just a few words regarding the general situation which Britain faces. What do the British people do to make their living? There are in the neighbourhood of forty-seven millions of them in a small island which has not the resources to support them. What do they have to do? Well, there are several lines of activities in which they engage to make their living. First of all, they produce what they can from .their own resources and they manufacture what they can from their own resources. Nest, they export as much goods as they can manage to manufacture and sell to pay for imports. Next, they depend on income from foreign investments. Next, they depend on income from carrying services which they have rendered with their merchant ships. Finally, they depend on the interest on financial loans and on insurance which the British have a good deal to do with.
What has happened to Britain? The Minister of Finance gave, I thought, a very fine and comprehensive picture of what has happened to Britain. He could have gone into great quantities of detail, which perhaps it was unnecessary to go into because hon. members, generally speaking, are well informed. But it would be a good thing to recall at this time that a tremendous amount of Britain's industrial capacity was destroyed during the last war. Many of the plants were actually bombed. A great number of British industries were changed over from a peacetime basis to a war-time basis; and the British were given as their part in the team the very task of changing their industries over from a peace-time basis to a war-time basis and were dependent upon the United States for their peace-time production. This is why the British were hurt so seriously when lease-lend was cancelled immediately at the close of the war.
Another important matter is this, that for about six years the youth of Great Britain have been trained in producing war material and consequently lack the skills and the facilities necessary to produce peace-time goods. Meanwhile a good many of the techniques in connection with peace-time production have been changed, so that even some who were skilled do not find themselves exactly qualified to produce at the present time. That is the first thing.

Then, with respect to British foreign investments, they have lost a tremendous amount of those foreign investments because they had to liquidate them to get raw materials with which to fight the war. Consequently, as the Minister of Finance points out, they can no longer depend on them to anything like the same degree as a source of income.
Then, at least one-third of the carrying ships of Great Britain have been destroyed in the war. They have been sunk or otherwise lost; they are not there; consequently the British are not able to use them as a means of deriving income.
This is only a part of all that has gone on. One could go into much greater detail. But the result of the whole study would be to show that the British capacity to produce goods is seriously impaired; and if we are to restore the British to the position in which they will be able to fight again in case they have the need to fight-and they may have to, in a very short time-we shall have to make every possible effort to see that they have the goods necessary to enable them to restore themselves to a high degree of productive capacity and financial strength.
What can Canada do about this whole matter? Some of us are beginning to suffer a little because of a shortage of goods, but I do not think many of us here in Canada have suffered much so far. There are some things we have to get along without. But the trouble in Great Britain is that the people have to get along without nearly all the things we enjoy. It is astonishing how seriously their diet is impaired. It must be borne in mind that these people have been enduring these conditions for five years. If we do not advance the goods to them they are going to have greater austerity than they had even during the war. How can one expect people who are impaired physically by malnutrition or undernutrition to be capable of a high measure of production. All that I am saying at the present time has quite obviously to do with defence. If Britain is to be strong and ready to fight again in case of need we must help to make her capable, and the only way to do that is to supply her with the goods which she cannot produce and which she can obtain only by trading exports for them.
I am going to sum up by making this statement. It is expedient that Canada should aid Britain to be strong. It is expedient that we should grant this loan, and greater loans still, if the British find that they need them. It is expedient that we should grant the loan so that Britain may be capable of being our ally

Loan to United Kingdom
in case of another war, that she may be a good market for Canada in times of peace, and that she may contribute to the general prosperity of mankind.
I am sure that every hon. member is well aware that many of the goods Britain produces are of extreme importance to the other nations of the world, and that there is a high demand in the world for those goods. The world cannot have as high a standard1 of living as is possible unless Britain is able to produce such goods. If, by reason of the want of a loan such as this, Britain cannot produce *those goods, the result will be an impairment of the general standard of living, of well-being and of prosperity throughout the world. The Minister of Finance pointed out that Britain was our A-l customer. She is indeed our A-l customer; and she was the A-l customer of thirty-one nations before the war. How many people know that? She imported more than any other nation of the goods produced by thirty-one countries. To what a tremendous ' extent, then, the general prosperity of the world depends upon the prosperity of Britain, and upon her capacity to import goods and to pay for them, must be obvious to all.
Finally, I think we all agree that Canada is able to lend the money. We may be afraid of the debt-I am afraid of the debt-but there are things we all dread more than debt; otherwise this house would not have sat calmly by and encouraged the government to incur fifteen billions of debt while the country was at war. Yes, Mr. Chairman, there are things we fear more than we fear debt, and there are things in the future that we need to fear more than we fear the debt that will be incurred. If we have to raise many billions as debt to pay for goods, as long as we are struggling with the present financial system, let us raise the money and supply the goods to Britain.
There is another aspect of the question that will have a strong appeal to every member of the house; that is the moral aspect. It is morally right that Canada should make this loan to Great Britain. In the first place, the war expenditures of Great Britain were proportionately greater than those of any other allied country. Everyone knows how we naturally react to the spectacle of any one member of the team bearing a heavier burden than the rest. It is beneath our national self-respect to allow Britain to continue to bear a greater burden financially than we are bearing.
Taxation in Britain was on a scale never before reached in any country in the world, I am told. Can we sit idly by and witness
such a state of affairs and do nothing about it and still feel that we can respect ourselves nationally?
Britain bore more than her shdre of the international financial burden of the war. She provided more goods on mutual aid to Russia, the United States and other nations of the world. She bore a greater international burden than any other one of the allied countries. Can we contemplate that without a twinge of conscience?
Britain faces a more difficult international trade position to-day than any other nation, as the minister has well pointed out. We naturally wish to help those whose ability has been impaired. Notice how readily, in any community, people contribute to the rebuilding of a home that has been destroyed by fire, especially when the sufferer is poor. Surely the same principle works internationally, especially when the country affected is a very close friend.

and certainly Britain has never done anything which should deprive her of a title to the friendship of the Canadian people. For the reasons I have outlined, M.r. Chairman, I wish to state, that the Social Credit group will enthusiastically support this loan to Britain.

Mr. Chairman, at the risk of being alone I wish to register my opposition to the principle embodied in the resolution. I do not propose to go into a detailed discussion of the principle of the bill which will be based on this resolution, but I desire to take this opportunity of expressing my strong opposition to that principle. I wish also to express sentiments that I have voiced in this house on previous occasions with reference to proposals of this kind.
History will have to take note of the fact that when it comes to the consideration of proposals relating to what is called the British empire there is no difference between one side of the house and the other. All the members of this House of Commons, with very few exceptions, always agree when a proposal is made to help to sustain the prestige, the grandeur and the prosperity of the United Kingdom.
We have heard during the last few days very beautiful words and strong expressions of opinion about Canadian citizenship. Well, if you bring these principles, these ideas, together with the sentiments that have been expressed this afternoon, under serious consideration, I think you will find a strong and a definite conflict of ideas and of principles.
Without any intention of offending the views or the sentiments of anyone in this house, I persist in calling this proposal
Loan to United Kingdom

another gift which is being made by the small fellow to the big fellow. The sum involved is, $1,250,000,000. What is that in the exchequer of the United Kingdom? A drop of water in the bucket, if not in the sea; and we get all excited about it, as if the whole world were going to crumble if we did not grant this new gift to a country which is ten times, fifty times richer than we are.
One has only to look at the map of the world to see the interests that the United Kingdom holds all over the globe wherever there is something of any value in the soil. This gift that we are proposing to make is out of proportion to our capacity for paying. The last speaker said that Britain was taxed to a higher degree than any other country, and he added, "I am told". If he will look at the figures he will discover that, in proportion, Canada is the most heavily taxed country of all those that participated in the war, and we had less interest than any other participating country. It is beyond our means, beyond our capacity, to make a gift of this kind at this particular time when we need so many things to help our country to recover from the false economy of the war to a reasonable and fair and durable economy for the time of peace.
We were told by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) who made an able speech-he is always impressive when he gets on his feet and argues on any question-that if we did not agree to this proposal we. might find ourselves between a financial organization at the head of which would be the United Kingdom, and the United States organization, and that Canada would be placed in a position to suffer very much if we did not agree to help the United Kingdom to revive her trade and to revive at the same time the whole trade of the world. I should like to hear any hon. member of this house state seriously that all that Canada did during the last war is to be lost if we do not agree to this last loan or gift that w'e are asked to make to the United Kingdom.
We were told by Britishers themselves that up to the present time Canada has done splendid work. Some of them have said, somewhat lightly, but with a large amount of truth: "We should not ask Canada to go any farther than what she has up to the present time, because the effort that Canada has made is beyond all expectation of any reasonable citizen, even of the United Kingdom." I do not propose for the moment to discuss certain arguments that have been advanced here. I reserve for a later day the right to go into more detail and make more compre-TMr. Cardin.]
hensive comparisons between our position and the position in which the United Kingdom finds itself at the present time. At the moment I do not want to delay the proceedings of the committee. If the resolution passes I ask that it be passed on division, because I do not agree with the principle embodied in it. I am convinced that there is no necessity, and no necessity has been shown, for Canada to enter into such an agreement on terms which are more favourable to the United Kingdom and more difficult for Canada than the terms of the. United States loan. We still have in our ears the voices of citizens of the United Kingdom advocating that the proposed United States loan should be refused. In the circumstances I wish to make my position clear and definite. In the past I have been opposed to the renewal of such gifts. At first they were properly described as gifts. Later on, they were called by another name-mutual aid. Now it is called a loan to be reimbursed in fifty years from now. Really it all amounts to the same thing.
The agreement contains a clause waiving all interest if at a certain period in the economic life of the United Kingdom they feel that they are not in a position to pay the interest. Well, I am opposed to that.
I think it is time that Canada took a definite step and spoke for herself instead of speaking for the British empire as we are doing all the time. Where is the Canadian spirit in this house? There is none.
A few days ago some hon. members spoke about hyphenated names. Heavens, if the bill which the Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) introduced to create a Canadian citizenship should pass, we shall be in the very same position of having a hyphenated name- Canadian citizen-British subject!
We are part of the British empire, and I claim, without any desire of offending the views of anyone, that we are not a sovereign country. We may be by strict interpretation of certain laws; but in practice we are to a large extent what we were before, colonials. We have somewhat increased the liberties /that we have enjoyed in the past; certain things are not imposed on us any more by the front door, but suggestions are made to us through the back door and we obey them. Those things happened during the last war and there are indications that they are still continuing throughout; the order is coming from outside in all things .relating to our economy, finances and commerce.
I am not afraid of the future of my country, even if my country is left alone. Even if my country is left between the sterling bloc and the United States I have enough confidence

Loan to United Kingdom
in Canada to feel that Canada is capable of coming through her difficulties and achieving a prominent place among the important nations of the world, even though she is not assisted by the one side or the other. Let us be ourselves; let us think for ourselves, and let us think of our future, the future of Canada. It is with these views, not complete I admit, and not the result of any preparation, that I express my opposition to the principle embodied in the resolution. I would agree to the passing of the resolution, but with the conventional term of "on division".

I should like to see the
resolution go through before six o'clock and the bill introduced. I compliment the government on this particular resolution. Notwithstanding what the preceding speaker has said, it follows out the principle laid down thirty years ago by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding when they offered aid to the mother country in the form of preferential trade, without asking anything in return. The resolution which precedes the bill will assist the mother country which suffered so terribly in the war.
Six o'clock.

I should like to see the resolution pass. The principle of the loan is exchange of goods and services for goods ' and services. It is not like the United States loan, exchange of goods and services for debt or gold. I should like to see the government go farther and offer further aid later on, and with what Australia and New Zealand have done to assist the mother country at this particular time, the United States loan could be done without. I should like to see the government thus go farther if necessary.
It is good business, first, last and all the time, as everybody will admit, because Britain was always our sure and best customer. The resolution has showrn what Canada has done.
It will give aid to the mother country as aid from Canada is being given France to recover herself.
In conclusion, I may say that under paragraph (d) I am glad Canada is cancelling the debt for the air scheme. I believe that is due the mother country. Our army, navy and air force were unprepared. Britain, save for the aid of the dominions, for two years prevented an invasion of our shores, which would have cost us much more than $400 million.
I hope the government when they borrow this sum of $1,250 million will do something to lessen the cost of these loans. As we know, we have paid heavily for some loans. We can borrow by private loans and negotiations,
or we can call for tenders. The fetter method has been proved most successful in Washington. We saw7 an example the other day where a company from Cleveland secured refunding at some cost of the debt of the whole city of Montreal.
I believe the people of Canada, Australia and New Zealand will rejoice to see that the dominions are as an economic unit, coming to the help of the mother country in her hour of trouble.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I have great admiration for the hon. member for Richelieu-Vereheres, but I am sorry that he has taken the stand which he has with regard to this particular resolution. As I see it, such a position will be regarded by others as though there was a division between us at a time when unity is necessary. We should hang together as we did during the war, and did so well, or we shall hang separately and the British empire will be no more.

The borrower who is advanced an interest-free loan, that is, a worthless investment which is nothing but a gift in disguise, is no longer required to be thankful since the shoe is now on the other foot and it behooves the benefactor to show gratitude. I am not ready to accept this argument, and I wanted to register my disapproval without delay, postponing until the second reading of the bill a mQre detailed discussion of my objections.
(Text).:

Mr. Chairman, I think a voice from the province of Quebec should be heard to-night in defence of the resolution before us. This resolution does not represent an entirely new policy of the Liberal party. In my view it is the continuation of a policy which was adopted during the war under dire exigencies.
I consider I have a right to discuss this matter because judgment has. been parsed upon it by the electorate of my constituency. "Billions to England" was the cry of every Nationalist, every member of the Bloc Populate and every independent member during the last election. In my own constituency the most forceful denunciator was the former member of parliament and he made many speeches. Previously he had separated from his party; after denouncing it in this house in the most violent terms, he crossed the floor of the chamber. During the campaign I defended the government to the best of my humble ability. The good people of the constituency of Rimouski had every opportunity to form an opinion. On polling day they gave their verdict and here I am to speak for them.
It seems to me that Canada's relations with the United Kingdom, even the purely commercial relations, are the greatest occasion for misunderstanding and misinterpretation. Our relations with other countries on

Loan to United Kingdom
approximately the same basis are not even questioned. Under the Export Credit Insurance Act loans have been authorized and made to other countries but never a word has been said. This afternoon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) tabled full details of all these loans. At the beginning of the session a question was asked and the answer appears in Hansard at page 358. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) asked for the details of loans and gifts made by Canada to other nations, and the following information
was given:
U.S.S.R	 $13,000,000
Norway	 13,000,000
Netherlands Indies	 15,000.000
Czechoslovakia	 19.000.000
Belgium	 25.000.000
China	 60,000.000
Netherlands	 125,000,000
France	 242,000,000
Total	 $512,000,000
These loans were considered by every nationalist as good business.
(Translation) :
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly.
Did those loans which you have just mentioned bear interest or were they interest-free?
According to the report of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) the interest rate ranges between 2| and 3 per cent.

He was not in the house this afternoon.
(Text):

If these loans were considered as purely business matters, I humbly submit that the present loan should be considered in the same way although it does involve a large amount of money. As was said by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Maedonnell), it should be appraised and judged solely in the light of the general interest of Canada and of its people. It should be judged from a purely selfish and egotistical point of view. In extending a loan a businessman or a man on the street has two things to consider. First, he must consider his own personal situation and. second, he must consider the solvency of the borrower. That is a good rule and it should be applied to the present case.
What is the financial situation of Canada? The statistics that I am about to give were obtained from the Canada Year Book for 1945. National income forms the fundamental basis of revenue. When national income is considered in relation to national revenue or taxes it faithfully portrays the economic
position of a country. From 1933, the darkest year of the depression, Canada's national income has risen from $2,795 million to an estimated amount of some $9,000 million for 1945. National revenue increased from some $500 million to a total of $2,765 million. There is no doubt that our national wealth is much greater in 1946 than it1 ever was. In using the other method of calculating national wealth, that of working back to capital values ough income tax returns, we find that the same assertion can be made.
Of course we must consider our national debt of some $15,000 million, most of which was incurred during the war and which therefore, is not represented by corresponding assets. However, this is counterbalanced to some extent by the fact that this loan is mainly held in Canada and is payable in Canadian funds. It is said that during the war Canada repatriated Canadian securities from the United Kingdom to a value of about $1,000 million and has accumulated sterling balances, later converted into a loan, of which there is still owing to Canada some $500 million which is guaranteed by liens on Canadian securities held in the ^United Kingdom. Therefore our financial situation as far as the United Kingdom is concerned has been converted to our advantage to the extent of $1,500 million. I think everyone who spoke before me concurred in the opinion that our financial situation is actually quite sound.
We have assumed great responsibilities to our own people. There is the interest on our debt, the reestablishment of our veterans, the payment of family allowances and so on. We must face great problems, such as reconversion, housing, great programmes of public works and railway expansion such as has been requested from the other side. After listening to many speeches in this house, I have formed the opinion that many of us are trying to raid the treasury in order to satisfy the demands of our own constituencies that this or that should be provided.
To meet these responsibilities, to solve these problems and to satisfy our constituents we shall need an annual revenue of some $2,000 million, and we shall have to get this from taxes. Taxes are derived from national income and the rate of taxation is in direct proportion to the national income. With a national income of $10,000 million, we must impose taxation at the rate of 20 per cent in order to raise $2,000 million. With an income of only $6,000 million the rate goes up 33i per cent. National income is the yardstick of the comparative severity of taxation. It is -a principle of economics that income results only from production. In that I agree
Loan to United Kingdom

Mr. Chairman, I am very glad to
speak on this measure following the hon. member for Rimouski. In the first place, I wish to congratulate the hon. member upon his wonderful address. I think he has presented his conception of the measure in a comprehensive and realistic manner. I was not going to participate in this debate but, like the hon. member for Rimouski, I feel that some voices from Quebec should be heard in favour of this measure.
This question merits thorough consideration and careful study. It has been explained clearly this afternoon by the Minister of Finance. We have heard about this measure for quite a while: now it is presented to the house in the form of a resolution. Later on, a bill will be introduced and we shall have a further opportunity to discuss the present measure.
I was very much surprised at the speech which was made at the end of the afternoon by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres. He stated at the beginning of his remarks that he was not very well prepared to speak on the matter but that he just wanted to state his opinion of the measure. When he said that, I recalled the advice which he had given to the people of Quebec about the seriousness of certain matters into which one should not go without careful study. I delved into some excerpts from the press, and I picked out this
Loan to United Kingdom

item, which appeared in the Montreal Star on ApMl 10, 1942, when the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres was addressing the people of Quebec on the matter of the plebiscite of 1942. He said:
I submit that several aspects of the question have not been presented to you, and, what is still more serious, you have not been shown the grave consequences which might result from your decision. It may very well be, in fact, that the vote to which you have pledged yourselves may bring results exactly contrary to those you desire.
I would be the last one to speak of this measure in emotional terms. It was a real comfort this afternoon to hear the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario state that he was considering this measure exclusively on the basis of the interests and the best interests of Canada itself. That is the tone that the Minister of Finance has set on this question, and that is the way that it is understood throughout Canada, that this loan is a good business proposition. But had there been anyone to suggest that the subject of this loan should be presented in emotional terms, I would again have recourse to thoughts expressed by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres as I found them in La Presse of Saturday, April 25, 1942, when he said, and I translate:
Independence would not protect us; on the contrary it would aggravate our obligations and the results of a possible defeat. Look at Belgium! Look at Holland! We are far from there, one might say. Yes. because the English fleet guards the ocean. But without it, what w-ould the defence of our coasts be worth?
These statements of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres should be remembered today. Were we considering this measure otherwise than as a business proposition; were we considering it as a gift, I would be entitled to consent to this measure, under the terms expressed by the hon. member himself, as a gift, and I would consent to it not with interest at two per cent but without any interest at all.	.
I agree with the hon. member for Rimouski that this measure is only one loan of a group of loans which have already been made in order to restore and maintain our export trade. In the debate on the speech from the throne at the beginning of the session the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg made it clear, and it has been made clearer since, that other loans have been made, about which hon. members who are opposing this measure have never uttered a word. I would repeat, although the hon. member for Rimouski has made it quite clear, what was pointed out by the member for Queens-Lunenburg. namely, that:
Loan agreements have been entered into with England. Belgium, China, Czechoslovakia, the Netherlands, the Netherlands East Indies, Norway and Russia. Furthermore, negotiations are well advanced toward making a very large amount of money available to France.
As part of that policy instituted by the government, in the best interests of Canada, we have this measure for a loan to the United Kingdom. We must understand that the economy of Canada and that of other countries interpenetrate. We cannot live alone. We must understand, in order to support this measure, that global strategy which the minister discussed so ably this afternoon.
The Liberal party is presenting this measure. It is supported by the Conservative party, by the C.C.F. and by the Social Credit party. A great deal of study was given to the question by the government before introducing the measure, and I do not see why certain individuals should rise and speak against the proposal after so many have given it careful consideration and so many people in all sections of the country, realizing what good business it is for Canada, have through their representatives, agreed to the resolution.
Again I will recall the words of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres when he declared in La Presse on Wednesday, January 12, 1938:
(Translation):
A man who stands alone in politics or in any organization is worth nothing at all. What can be expected of an individual who is always changing about and who has such a nasty character he can get along with no one? Personally, I do not trust anyone who is neither with the government nor with the opposition, and is regarded as a one-man party.
' (Text):
I know that hon. members are anxious to have this debate concluded and I have no desire to take up any more of the time of the house. Let me say, in conclusion, that I have confidence, in the government of the country, and knowing that in every move it makes it does consider the best interests of Canada, I wish on behalf of my constituents to declare that I am very happy to support this measure since I believe that its object is to safeguard the interests of the country.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Usley thereupon moved for leave to introduce bill No. 28, respecting the financial agreement between Canada and the United Kingdom signed on the sixth day of March, 1946.

speechtext:
I should like first of all to say a few words on the Japanese question. I do not wish to dwell very long on that particular aspect of the subject, but I will place myself squarely behind the British Columbia members who have preceded me in this debate. The people of British Columbia are very much concerned over the delay in the application of the policy announced by the government. It seems to me that the government must recognize that delay will bring them further and further into difficulties, and they must very soon come to a decision and carry through their policy.
The government will be more and more under the influence of pressure groups in this connection. I would point out to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), when he receives these pressure groups, that the contest, if there is one, is between the people of British Columbia represented by their members in parliament, who have a responsibility not only to themselves but also to those whom they represent, and those deputations that have a responsibility only to themselves. The people of British Columbia have borne this Japanese problem for many years and for them it might be likened to a red-hot shot. During the war, after years of effort, they succeeded in dumping it on the lap of this government. There is only one thing that the people of British Columbia will not accept, and that is to have this red-hot shot dumped back into their hands to carry it again alone.
So that whatever policy the government eventually decides to adopt-and I hope that it will adopt a policy quickly-that policy cannot be one of forcing back upon us a load which we have carried too long and know too well. That is all I wish to say about the Japanese.
I now turn to the bill itself. First, I should like to refer to the point raised by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke) and the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen). I was veiy much surprised that in introducing the bill the Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) did not make any statement as to the discussions he had had with Great Britain and the other members of the commonwealth. I should have thought
that in connection with a bill of such importance nothing could be more desirable than that there should be such a discussion; and if the Secretary of State were to take the view I do, surely he would have made that announcement when he introduced the bill. Then, arising out of his remarks in reply to the hon. member for York South (Mr. Cockeram), I wish to say that certainly for many years no one on this side of the house has doubted Canada's absolute sovereignty. Certainly there will be no one in the official opposition who will regret that we are taking the lead in the development of empire affairs. But if we are to take such a lead it is of vital importance to a very large number of people in this country that the lead we take and the example we set to the other nations of the commonwealth shall be not only for the good of Canada but also to the advantage of that association which so many of us believe is good for Canada. Therefore, if this bill is to be used as a model for legislation in other countries of the commonwealth it is vital that we do not put any impediment in the way of the free movement of peoples in the empire family.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: Does this bill do that?

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: In the five years residence rule it certainly does.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: That has been the law for twenty-seven years.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
I shall leave that point and come to another angle of this matter. I am a natural-born Canadian whose forbears were also born in this country. I am entirely Canadian, and I am one of a very large number who are entirely Canadian, yet who say with pride, "I am a British subject." Therefore, I think I may speak for a moment on behalf of that very large class. The Canadian-born British subject is the one class of Canadian that has taken an awful beating in this debate. We have heard much about the glories of all other classes of Canadians, while the Canadian-born who is proud to be a British subject has been accused of various weaknesses in his Canadianism. Well, I think it is very good that matters of this kind should be brought up, because the opinion of others is very good for one's soul. Until this debate I had never realized that my Canadianism was not complete. I do not doubt that it is, even after what has been said, but certainly it will do me good to know there are those who hold such a view.
I welcomed the bill heartily, and I welcome it particularly for the reasons so ably advanced by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll).

Canadian Citizenship
I consider that this bill is of tremendous importance, as the hon. member said, to the class of Canadians on whose behalf he spoke; and I can well understand the view he takes when he says many people who have come into this country have not experienced the same sense of nationhood they knew in their native countries in crowded Europe. But I wish to say to the hon. member for Spadina, who, I am sorry, is not in his seat now, that he must not doubt the attachment of native-born Canadians to their birthright. We travel in' no shadow of the mother country or of the United States. We are British subjects because and only because we are Canadians; we are not. British subjects in spite of being Canadians. The hon. member spoke of "soft, apologetic Canadianism." I must say I have not experienced any such feeling, nor have I ever encountered it in this country. Very often I have met the reverse of soft, apologetic Canadianism, but never that type.
In addition to welcoming the bill, I welcome this debate, during which many frank things have been said. That is a good thing. I have sat silently in this house for some months now and have been amazed and distressed at references to colonialism and slurs on the status of British subjects. I have not been silent because 11 agreed with those remarks, but rather because I <jlid not understand and therefore did not know how I could answer them. In this debate, however, I think I have heard the reasons which motivated references to colonialism and derogatory remarks about British subjects; and if I do understand them now I might say a word in reply. I gathered from the speeches of the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Rinfret) and the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond) that both hon. gentlemen were of the opinion, although in very different degree, that the status of a British subject meant there was some allegiance to Great Britain or Great Britain's laws as well as allegiance to Canada. If that is so I think I can answer it. I would say that such a view is a complete misconception of law and of fact; and since it is only a misconception that stands between us, nothing really holds us apart. I say perfectly frankly that if dual nationality or allegiance to another country existed owing to my being a British subject; if it meant that Canada was not a sovereign state, I would join with my hon. friends not in destroying the status of a British subject but rather in rectifying it, so that if there were derogations from Canada's sovereignty those derogations would be removed. I wish to say this-and I do not say it for myself, but for all Canadians proud of the status of British subjects-that that

status is not to us one of habit or law, or one to be supported simply because we were born to it; it is a status we honour because we believe in it.
We believe in the status of British subject, and as Canadians wish to remain British subjects, because to us the British Empire or the British Commonwealth of Nations, whichever you like to call it, has been for many years in the past, and will be for many years in the future, the greatest bulwark of freedom that exists in this world. We desire to remain British subjects. We are proud of being British subjects now, because to be and to continue to be such is to us the surest way to be and to continue to be free men.
If there was any such misconception that I thought I gathered in the speeches of the hon. members to whom I have referred, it seems to me that the misconception might be based simply upon our use of words. I would point out to the house that where we can refer to citizens of Canada as Canadians or citizens of Brazil as Brazilians, we cannot refer to citizens of the United States of America by any adjectival addition to that country's name. Therefore we call them Americans, although they have no greater right so to be called than have we or the Brazilians. After all, we live in America and we, too, are Americans. But we allow to the United States, for convenience, the national appelation of American.
The same might be said about Great Britain. That country is not Britain; it is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and one cannot add to that description ,the suffix "an" and use it conveniently in conversation.
Therefore, particularly in the United States, there has grown up a habit, which I noticed in the debate this afternoon, of referring to the citizens of Great Britain or of the United Kingdom as "the British". Surely that gives rise to a misconception of the term "British". Surely we are imparting to the citizens of Great Britain a status they do not exclusively possess, and that they do not claim exclusively for themselves.
They are not the only British. A British subject is not a citizen of Great Britain, as one hon. member has suggested. I suggest to anyone who doubts that statement that he ask an Englishman what his nationality is. He will say that it is English. And if one were to confuse a Welshman with an Englishman I think there would be a great row from the Welshman.

Canadian Citizenship
To drive that point home I would call the attention of the house to the perfect conception of nationality which exists in Scotland where, not only would the Scot be annoyed if he were called an Englishman-I would not dare do it-but also Scotland, although part of the United Kingdom, still has its own law, and still jealously retains many of the attributes of a separate country. So that I do not for a moment think it ran be said, with any justification, that a British subject is something which pertains exclusively to Great Britain.
I wish to enlarge upon my conception of the status of British subject. As I said. I am a Canadian and I come from a family which through all Canada's history, long before confederation, has lived in Canada. I have no connection whatsoever with Great Britain. Yet I am a British subject. As a British subject, however, I am not the subject of any nation but Canada. And let me say here, with all sincerity, that no nation holds a greater place in my heart than my own country of Canada.
A British subject, therefore, is not a citizen of the United Kingdom. He is a citizen, rathe, of the British commonwealth of nations. A British subject has one king and one country-not two countries. But he has fraternal affiliations with many countries; he is close to being a world citizen. He is a member of the greatest collection * of freely associated nations the world has ever seen. He is an internationalist in a world which is still nationalist, but is groping toward internationalism. He is a member of the first successful united nations organization. I say to the house that the British subject is the prime hope for the future of a free world.
The term is the exclusive possession of no one country, but rather it is the joint possession of many. Although I do not wish to labour this, I might offer another illustration of status, which I think makes it very clear. The hon. member for Outremont and I are both British subjects from Canada. Likewise, an Australian is a British subject from Australia. Mr. Churchill is a British subject from England and Field Marshal Smuts is a British subject from South Africa. Neither Mr. Churchill nor Field Marshal Smuts has any greater claim to the title "British subject" than has any hon. member in the house. Country of origin gives no precedence whatever to that appellation.
Let us for a moment turn to the bill. If the status of British subject is as I have described it, then it is something very much to be prized. It represents freedom; it represents
sovereignty, and at the same time it represents the ability to join with other countries in something more than a mere arrangement of convenience for the time being.
When a British subject comes from England to Canada he may, under this bill, if he wishes, remain a British subject from England or, by going through the procedure provided in the bill, he may become a British subject from Canada. If he follows the latter course he assumes allegiance to the law of Canada and at the same time renounces his allegiance to the domestic law of England. Therefore I say he does not become naturalized in the usual sense of the term, but rather he becomes re-nationalized. If that is his status, if the process that he has gone through is different, why should he be lumped together in this bill and be forced to go through exactly the same procedure as must be gone through by an alien? The hon. member for Nanaimo -(Mr. Pearkes) pointed out the other day, I think most cogently, that the period of apprenticeship should not necessarily be the same for the one who has already partaken of a part of our joint heritage and who needs only to familiarize himself with our domestic law in order to be able to fit very well into our national life. That he should be lumped together with the alien is, to my mind, an ungracious act by a government wThich has not paid sufficient attention to that non-vocal but very large number of people in this country for whom I think I can claim to speak. I say it is an ungracious act because it. is an unnecessary act and also because, as far as I know, it is a unilateral act.
At the opening of my remarks I referred to the necessity of consultation with the other nations of the commonwealth before introducing this bill. If we are setting an example to those other nations we must be clear in >ur minds as to what we are doing if we lump these people together in the cause of sovereignty. I say to the Secretary of State that sovereignty is not something over which to chuck your weight about. I say rather that sovereignty is pure, steady power which needs vivid expression only when it is actually attacked.
I do not think there is anyone in this country or in this house who doubts Canada's absolute sovereignty to-day. We hear about appeals to the privy council and the right to amend our own constitution. But do not let us think that the existence of those limitations on our sovereignty, if they can be called such, are there because of any act committed outside the boundaries of this country. We all know, and if it were not so I would be

Mr. Speaker, I do not agree by any means with many statements which have been made so far in this debate, and for that reason I shall ask the indulgence of the house for a few moments.
We are now dealing with bill No. 7, an act respecting citizenship, nationality, naturalization and status of aliens, which is now referred to as the Canadian Citizenship Act. This bill had its first reading some three weeks ago, on March 31. It is divided into seven parts and forty-seven sections, and the principles of the bill are directly related to about seven different items. It deals with ' natural-born Canadian citizens, Canadian citizens other than natural-born, loss of Canadian citizenship, status of citizens and recognition of British subjects, status of aliens, and the method of procedure and evidence, as well as a schedule defining the oath of allegiance.
This bill is undesirable for the reason that it takes away from British subjects a privilege which they have had and which they enjoy to-day.

I will tell the minister, if he will follow me. If this bill passes as recommended by the Secretary of State, it will mean that British, subjects throughout the empire will probably go to Australia or New Zealand in preference to Canada. This bill has been the sounding-board and is the instru-

ment to make known to this house and to Canada that there is in this house an antiBritish following who are not desirous of giving preference to British subjects.
I welcome the opportunity to say something on this bill. The statement has been made, with reference to Japanese now domiciled in Canada, that the predicament and the embarrassing position in which the government now finds itself may be relieved by the passing of this bill. I wonder whether the bringing forward of this measure at the present time has any bearing on the Japanese question.

speechtext: All right. Some supporters of the government could not avoid blushing to hear the various anti-British expressions which have already been used in this debate. After the next few months, when the troops have returned home from overseas and are settled in civilian life, Canadian immigration policy will likely be relaxed to admit many British people who are desirous of coming to this country. speechtext:
It has. Let the minister follow me. I should like to draw to his attention the immigration set-up as it existed in the ten years following 1930. There entered into Canada about 150,000 annually, or, in that decade, a total of one and a half million immigrants. One hundred thousand annually were aliens and the other fifty thousand annually were from Great Britain and the empire, or put it in this way, for every three immigrants entering Canada one was British and two were of foreign extraction. In the same period we lost 100,000 citizens annually to the United States. This means that the best citizens Canada produced, boys and girls of Canadian families, educated in our collegiate institutes, our technical schools and our universities, went across the border to find positions for themselves and their families. For every British immigrant entering Canada two Canadian citizens went to the United States. This is a state of affairs which we

should not allow to occur again. Just as our immigration policy in that period was antiBritish, so is this proposed bill, and I tell the Secretary of State that we have already had two indications of a government attempting to pilot through the house-this most contentious bill. A citizenship bill was introduced by a previous secretary of state, Hon. C. H. Cahan, in 1931, but it was withdrawn, and-

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: It was not the same bill at all.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
I know it was not the same bill, but it had to do with citizenship. The urgency to-day is no greater than it was at that time. Two other contentious bills, one dealing with the flag and the other seeking to abolish Dominion day, have already been brought forward this session. I would refer particularly to the procedure in dealing with the Canada day bill, which was sponsored by a private member and was oiloted successfully through the house in one .afternoon and evening. The present bill is also contentious, and I tell the Secretary of State that he might have been well advised to have left this to the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Cote) who did such a good job in support of the government.
Though it has been recalled recently, I would briefly refer to the part played by Great Britain in world war I and world war II. In world war I Russia was an ally, but dropped out before the war was finished. In world war II she did not enter untfl after the war had continued for months. In'world war I France was on the side of Britain; in world war II she capitulated to Germany nine months after the war commenced. The United States did not enter either world war I or world war II until some -time after those wars commenced. In the last war Great Britain and the empire stood alone against Germany for over a year. This must not be forgotten. This is not a time for the House of Commons to enact legislation taking from British subjects entering Canada the rights they have enjoyed for generations. British subjects throughout the world should not be placed for immigration purposes in the same category as aliens who fought against the empire.
May I recall to the house something which Canada should not overlook, the part played by her troops on at least two occasions. Canada declared war in August, 1914, and September, 1939. Canada owes much to those men who in 1914 and 1939 formed the first and second divisions. The majority of these men were of British stock. If I may make a personal reference, I remember well, as do some other

Canadian Citizenship
members of this house, the first inspection by Their Majesties of the first Canadian division on a Saturday afternoon in November, 1914, on Salisbury plain. With Their Majesties the King and Queen were Lord Roberts and Lord Kitchener. I wish to mention particularly the Princess Pats. The majority of these men were South African veterans who freely volunteered to serve Canada and the empire. They were marked by the ribbons they wore. The key men in nearly every section, company and brigade were veterans. A few weeks later, in April, 1915, the same troops, at Ypres, when the Germans launched their famous first gas attack, made a name for Canada, and from that very moment Canada's prestige in the empire has steadily grown.
What happened in 1914 repeated itself in 1939. The men of the first and second divisions were veteran volunteers, the majority being of British stock.
Let us also not forget that it was the British navy in the fall of 1914 and in 1939 that delivered Canada's first division safely to England. Reference was made to that a few minutes ago in the loan debate, and I shall not refer to it at length. But I would say this. Deputations from Canada have visited the empire year in and year out since confederation. Even since the last session representatives of Canada were in England. The part which our Canadian soldiers overseas played in world war I and world war II has done more to cement Canada to the empire than all the deputations and conferences held before or since.
Let me give one illustration. We had in Kingston a unit of the empire air training scheme, No. 14, which was the first and largest fleet air training school in Canada. There were 100 classes of about fifty each, which meant 5,000 men training there for the R.A.F. fleet air arms. These boys served in the most hazardous branch of the service. What happened during these four years? Many of them, not dozens but scores of them married Canadian girls. Many went overseas and many of them wish to return to Canada. Why should those boys be placed ini the same category as aliens who have to wait for five years before being granted the franchise? No finer citizens will enter Canada than the 30,000 or 40,000 war brides who wish to find new homes here at the present time. We must not overlook the thousands of Canadian brides who married British soldiers and soldiers of our allies and who would like to return to Canada.

For five years. Since the last session of parliament Canada was represented by members of the government in London. Heading the deputation were the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Martin). What happened there? Apparently the Secretary of State was not too favourably impressed by Canada's relationship and responsibility to the mother country. We have him returning from the old country, and the first major piece of legislation, contentious as it is, is tabled and sponsored in his name. He evidently set out to discard British preference in regard to British immigration.
Tuesday last developed into a Japanese and British Columbia day. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) did not hesitate to state where he differed with the government on this bill. The fact that bill No. 7 has been sponsored by the government makes it difficult, if not impossible, for government supporters to take any other position than a party view of it. This afternoon I went into the library and looked up the Globe and Mail, because I happened to be in London in 1937 during the conference there. We have heard a good many things said in connection with this bill and something flashed through my mind regarding what had taken place at that conference. I am sorry I have not the clipping because I did not know that I would be referring to the matter at this moment. However, take the Globe and Mail for the month of May, 1937, and you will find that at that conference the statesmen were dealing with the question of citizenship, which occupied a great deal of their time. On that occasion the premier of South Africa shot

a question at the meeting which took them all by surprise. He wanted to know what the definition of "British subject" was and no one could answer him. A committee was appointed and a former Minister of Justice was made chairman, while the British attorney general, whose name has slipped my memory, spoke for twenty-five minutes on the subject of British citizenship. After the discussion was over, they did not seem to be much farther ahead. What took place in 1937 at that conference only convinces us that this citizenship bill is a contentious one and something that should not be rushed through the house hurriedly but should be studied from all angles.
