I
should like to contribute a few words to the discussion of this bill. I am absolutely in support of the principle of it. As a child I had my education partly in the old country,, in Scotland, and here, also in this country. I think a lot of the race I come from in Scotland, but I also think a great .deal of the country in which I was born, Canada., I also realize that this country comprises many men and nationalities and that here we still have to write down, when we are asked to furnish information on going to the United States on a visit, that we are British subjects. We are still known by our racial origin, and it is about time that this country grew up and that we became just Canadians.
In the United States, no matter whether a man be an Italian or a Czechoslovakian, he is always an American and there is no deviation from that. We here in Canada should have the same spirit and be known as Canadians.
The tradition of the old country has in some respects held back the development of this country in so far as working-class conditions are concerned. I am now referring to the merchant marine. In the building of freighters, which we1 constructed during the war, 10,000-tonners, we followed the good old British traditions of putting the galley amidships and the mess hall at the front of the boat, and you had to lug the food across the open deck. Imagine what it would be like in the middle of winter on the north Atlantic I An American would have enough sense to put the galley and the mess hall in one part, but we have to follow the tradition of the British nary and the time of Lord Nelson.
That may be a small thing, but it means a great deal to the men working on the ship. I suggest that we here should establish our own traditions on the North American continent. I am not so much concerned about a national viewpoint. I am thinking of the spirit of the people of the whole North

American continent. It is something distinctive and we should follow along our own lines.
There has also been too great a tendency on the part of those who have been British-born or who have come of British stock to rub it into the other fellow. I shall never forget the time I was working on a threshing outfit in southern Alberta. There I saw Dutchmen, Belgians, Czechoslovakians and Poles. One Englishmen had preceded me on the job and he claimed that he was the only white man there. That is the sort of thing that must stop if we expect to have a united nation.
In the speeches that have been made on this bill, especially by members from British Columbia, hon. gentlemen seem to have suffered from violent attacks of yellow fever. I come from Skeena, a federal riding, a fishing district which produces as much fish as any riding in that province, and in spite of the Jap issue they elected me. Let me explain the reason they did so. They found out a long time ago what was the secret of it. Like the other members from British Columbia I am absolutely opposed to the Japs going back to the doast, but for a reason. In the last election, if it had not been for the Jap ifesue the poor Conservatives and Liberals would not have known what to talk about: they would have been absolutely bankrupt. The fishermen on that coast suffered during the depression; fish went down to around two cents a pound, and the full hatred of the fishermen was turned to the' Japs, their fellow workers. But when the crisis begins to become apparent in this system, as it will with mathematical certainty, I hope there will be -no Japs on the coast on whom to blame it. This time the people will know the cause of the trouble.
I went back to British Columbia during the last provincial campaign. The last lone Liberal there, Mr. Pattullo, was in desperate circumstances. He came out with this line of propaganda, that if the C.C.F. got in they would allow' the big companies to bring the Japanese back into the canneries. It was my duty to tell the people that if the C.C.F. .got in there would be no big fish packing companies. But he lost, and again the Japanese were the main issue in that area.
What I want to see brought out clearly is that there is no difference among the workers in this country, whether we be black or yellow or red. We all suffer under the same system, and soon we are going to realize that. Sir James Orr says that in a couple of years we shall have complete collapse of commodity prices unless such prices are fixed internationally. If that collapse becomes apparent

on the coast within the next two years the fishermen will realize once and for all who are the real Japs. A year before the election I attempted to go on the radio with a speech in which I wanted to say that after the war with Japan was over and won our first act would be to put Hirohito back on the throne. The C.B.C. censor, who said that he was not a censor but that he just checked things, censored that speech and said that such a statement was seditious. I was in the army, and he was not; but they did put Hirohito back [DOT] on the throne, and these governments here did trade with Hirohito even after we had declared war on Germany. Therefore in the final analysis, putting Hirohito back on the throne showed more of a community of interest with the ruling class of Japan than with their own workers here.
This citizenship bill is a step in the right direction. I hope it will mark the beginning of a united Canada.

I did not really expect to be called on to speak to-night, Mr. Speaker; I thought there was a long list ahead of me, but I do not want to miss the opportunity of saying a word or two on this particular measure. It is not very often that one in this corner of the house is able to agree so wholeheartedly with the present government, but I wish to congratulate the government and the Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) on this bill. It is peculiar to note that at infrequent intervals during the life of this government they have shown flashes of brilliance, but their inspiration has come from only one source. Many years ago there sat in this house, with a smaller group an,d under a somewhat different name but with just about the same philosophy, a gentleman from Winnipeg named Mr. Woodsworth. He was keen to have the old age pension brought into effect, and as a result of his constant pressure the Liberal government of that time finally gave us old age pensions. They were not very good ones, but still it indicated that the government were susceptible to such propositions after a great deal of pressure, and, of course, if they thought it would do them good politically. Then, after another long period, following constant pressure by progressive people on this side of this house and throughout the country- I did not say Progressive Conservatives but progressive people-the same government finally brought in the family allowances measure. That was another good step; the allowances were not good enough, but they were far better than nothing at all.
I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is to be commended for the selection of his Secretary of State (Mr. Martin). I do not make that statement in order to obtain any applause either for myself or for the minister, but simply to point out that apparently the hon. gentleman is open to inspiration, and is able to convince the government that something good should be adopted. He has now brought in this citizenship bill. I wish to read from a little pamphlet; and then I will give the name of it.
The C.C.P. again pledges itself to . . . the adoption of a distinctive national flag and national anthem and the necessary legal provision
for Canadian citizenship.
This little book is called the "C.C.F. Manifesto", and was drawn up at the C.CJF. national convention held in Montreal a year ago last November and early December. So that the government can be congratulated on being able to accept suggestions of this kind, and on being able to select from the platform, of another party the things they consider good. We hope that some day they may take more from our platform; in fact we believe it would be an extremely good thing if they would read this little book all the way through and adopt everything it suggests.
To Canadian-born citizens like myself I believe this measure is very welcome. I welcome it not only for reasons of national pride, because a perspn should not have too much national pride just because he was born here. I cannot be proud o'f being born here because I had nothing to do with it, but can feel very lucky to have been born in a country like Canada and to have grown up among the kind of people we have here, those who were born here and those who have come here from other lands. I believe those who like myself were born here will welcome this for another reason. As I grew up I made up my mind that never, under any circumstances, no matter what the law says-and I am a law-abiding citizen-would I ever give any nationality to any government official on any question but that of Canadian; and I never have. I do not know whether I can be arrested for breaking that law, but I make the statement that I have never given any other nationality than Canadian, and if this bill should not pass I will still stick to that. No one will ever get me to say anything else without putting me in a torture chamber. I could not do anything else; I have to be a Canadian' or I am nothing at all, and I refuse to accept that alternative.

Possibly the people who can be proudest of this bill are those who have come here from other shores. They at least can say they exercised their intelligence and chose the country in which they wanted to live. Their coming here has been a compliment to Canada, a compliment to those who were born here and a compliment to their own intelligence in wanting to live here. They have made a great contribution to this country, and I am sure they must feel gratified, after having chosen to come to these shores, that now they will be able to call themselves what they wanted to be.
So far as the Japanese question is concerned, let me say that I am not closely associated with it at the present time. However, I should like to tell hon. members from British Columbia, from whichever side of the house they come, that I remember the question quite well around thirty-five years ago when I was a very young man. I was working in British Columbia then for wages, and I remember that when the. Japanese came in there at that time they were welcomed by the employers.

But let me say this to the house, that there is one elderly Canadian gentleman of Japanese origin who sits with me in the Canadian legion, a veteran of the last war, of the Princess Patricia Canadian Light Infantry. That same Canadian Japanese citizen is liked by all the Canadian legionnaires around there. He is received and accepted in all circles, the same as any other individual out there. But he is a practical farmer, a good farmer. He has a wife and family, and one of his boys was killed in the Canadian forces in this war. Does anyone here think for one moment that I am ever going to cast a vote which will throw a reflection upon that land of individual? It certainly would not be fair to do so. That is the way I feel about these people.
This bill carries with it a great many privileges and responsibilities. One of those privileges is the right to vote, and the responsibility is the obligation to vote and to try to understand what one is voting on. Those are two things which go with oitizbnship, and should not be forgotten.
The fact that the bill, as described by the Secretary of State, is to provide for some kind of ceremony and initial training for these people to teach them the responsibilities connected with their privileges is all to the good. I believe the newcomers will welcome it, and be the better for it.
They have another privilege, the right to do useful work. That is an important privilege in the citizenship of any country-the right to work at useful work. They have no right to be thrown on the bread-line every so often when the system under which we operate refuses to work. If they are to be citizens they have the right to work. Then they have the obligation to accept useful work. Their jobs should be there, and they have the right to take them, and also the obligation.
. They have the right to education and training to make them more useful in some useful job and to make them useful and valuable citizens in the community. They have the right to training to the extent of their ability to learn that to which their training is directed. They have the obligation which goes with that, that of educating themselves

The Governor General
to the best of their ability, according to the facilities made available to them for that purpose. That is a privilege and a responsibility, right there.
They have the right to security and comfort to the fullest extent of Canada's ability to produce the goods and services needed for security and comfort, regardless of their ability to work. That is right in line with the resolution placed before the house by an hon. member opposite.
With that obligation goes the obligation of all citizens, whether they were born here, or whether they came here later, or are newcomers recently arrived, of contributing to the comfort and security of the less fortunate among our citizens.
If this citizenship bill will impress upon the people the fact that these privileges are accompanied by obligations, then I think we have one of the measures to which the people of Canada have been looking forward for a long time. Let me again remind the house that this was part of the programme of the party to which I belong, of hon. members sitting in this corner of the house. Because of that, and for other reasons I have mentioned, I believe there will be no difficulty in our supporting the measure.
